w: I (sodium) fills 1s, 2s and 2p before 3s: a ground state. II puts an electron in 3s while 2p holds only 5, so it is an excited state of neon. III (potassium) fills 3p and then 4s, which comes before 3d: a ground state. The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is a ground state. After 3p, the next sublevel to fill is 4s, not 3d.
Statement II is not a ground state. The 2p sublevel is not full, yet an electron sits in 3s.
Statement II is not a ground state. An electron moved up to 3s before 2p was full.

q:
Which are chemical changes?
I. Ice melting on a warm day
II. An iron nail rusting
III. A log burning in a fireplace
h: A chemical change makes a new substance. A change of state keeps the same substance.
w: I is a physical change: melted ice is still H2O. II is a chemical change: iron reacts with oxygen to form a new substance, rust. III is a chemical change: burning turns wood into CO2, water and ash. The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement III is also a chemical change. Burning makes new substances such as carbon dioxide and ash.
Statement I is a physical change. Melted ice is still water.
Statement I is a physical change. A change of state does not make a new substance.

q:
Which formulas are paired with their correct names?
I. FeCl3, iron(III) chloride
II. N2O4, dinitrogen tetroxide
III. CaCl2, calcium dichloride
h: Prefixes such as di- and tetra- are used only for compounds of two nonmetals. A metal that can form more than one ion gets a Roman numeral.
w: I is correct: iron forms more than one ion, and three Cl− ions balance Fe3+, so the name is iron(III) chloride. II is correct: N2O4 contains two nonmetals, so prefixes are used. III is wrong: CaCl2 is ionic and is named calcium chloride, with no prefix. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement I is correct. Three Cl⁻ ions balance one Fe³⁺ ion, and iron needs a Roman numeral.
Statement III is wrong. Ionic compounds such as CaCl₂ do not use prefixes.
Statement III is wrong. Calcium compounds are ionic, so the name has no di prefix.

q:
Which statements about 1.00 mol of water, H2O (18.02 g/mol), are true?
I. It contains 6.02 × 1023 hydrogen atoms.
II. It has a mass of 18.02 g.
III. It contains 6.02 × 1023 molecules.
h: One mole of molecules is 6.02 × 10²³ molecules. Each H₂O molecule has two H atoms.
w: I is false: each molecule has 2 H atoms, so there are 2 × 6.02 × 1023 = 1.20 × 1024 H atoms. II is true: the mass of 1 mol in grams equals the molar mass. III is true: 1 mol of anything is 6.02 × 1023 units. The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement I is false. Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms, so the number of H atoms is doubled.
Statement II is true. The mass of one mole in grams equals the molar mass.
Statement I is false. Count the hydrogen atoms in one H₂O molecule.

q:
Three samples each have a mass of 10.0 g. Rank them from fewest moles to most moles.
I. H2 (2.02 g/mol)
II. O2 (32.00 g/mol)
III. H2O (18.02 g/mol)
h: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass. With equal masses, a larger molar mass gives fewer moles.
w: I: 10.0 ÷ 2.02 = 4.95 mol. II: 10.0 ÷ 32.00 = 0.313 mol. III: 10.0 ÷ 18.02 = 0.555 mol. From fewest to most: II < III < I. For the same mass, the heaviest molecule gives the fewest moles.
x: This order is reversed. Equal masses of a light gas such as H₂ give many more moles than a heavy one.
Sample III has more moles than sample II. Divide 10.0 g by each molar mass and compare.
This order follows molar mass upward. A larger molar mass gives fewer moles, not more.

q:
Which molecules are polar?
I. HCl
II. CCl4
III. CH4
h: A molecule is polar when it has polar bonds whose dipoles do not cancel. A tetrahedral molecule with four identical atoms around the center is symmetric.
w: I is polar: H–Cl is a polar bond, and there is no other bond to cancel it. II is nonpolar: the four C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel. III is nonpolar: C–H bonds are nearly nonpolar, and the shape is symmetric. The answer is I only.
x: Statement II is nonpolar. Its four C–Cl dipoles are arranged symmetrically and cancel.
Statement II has polar bonds, but its tetrahedral shape makes the bond dipoles cancel.
Statement III is nonpolar. C–H bonds are nearly nonpolar, and the molecule is symmetric.

q:
Which molecules contain a triple bond in their Lewis structure?
I. N2
II. HCN
III. C2H2
h: Draw each Lewis structure. Each C needs four bonds, and each N needs three bonds plus one lone pair.
w: I: N≡N gives each N an octet. II: H–C≡N gives C four bonds and N an octet. III: H–C≡C–H gives each C four bonds. All three, I, II and III, need a triple bond.
x: Statement II also has a triple bond. Carbon needs four bonds, and only one of them goes to H.
Statement III also has a triple bond. Each C in C₂H₂ has one H, so it needs three bonds to the other C.
Statement I also has a triple bond. Each N needs three shared pairs to complete its octet.

q:
Which processes are exothermic (release heat)?
I. Liquid water freezing
II. Ice melting
III. Methane burning in a gas stove
h: Forming attractions between particles, as when a liquid freezes, releases energy. Pulling particles apart, as in melting, absorbs energy.
w: I is exothermic: water releases heat to its surroundings as it freezes. II is endothermic: melting ice absorbs heat. III is exothermic: combustion releases heat, which is why we burn fuel. The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement I is exothermic too. Water gives off heat to its surroundings as it freezes.
Statement II is endothermic. Ice must absorb heat to melt.
Statement II is endothermic. Melting takes in heat.

q:
A balloon holds a fixed amount of gas. Which changes would increase its volume?
I. Raising the temperature at constant pressure
II. Raising the pressure at constant temperature
III. Lowering the pressure at constant temperature
h: Volume is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature (Charles's law) and inversely proportional to pressure (Boyle's law).
w: I is true: by Charles's law, the volume increases as the temperature increases. II is false: by Boyle's law, a higher pressure squeezes the gas into a smaller volume. III is true: a lower pressure lets the gas expand. The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III also increases the volume. Pressure and volume are inversely related.
Statement I also increases the volume. Heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand.
Statement II decreases the volume. Pressure and volume are inversely related.

q:
According to the kinetic molecular theory, which statements about gases are true?
I. Gas particles stop moving at 0 °C.
II. Gas particles are far apart compared with their own size.
III. The average kinetic energy of gas particles increases as the temperature increases.
h: 0 °C is 273 K, far above absolute zero. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles.
w: I is false: 0 °C is 273 K, and particles keep moving at any temperature above absolute zero (0 K). II is true: most of a gas's volume is empty space. III is true: average kinetic energy is proportional to the Kelvin temperature. The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement II is true. Gas particles are tiny compared with the empty space between them.
Statement I is false. 0 °C is 273 K, and gas particles are still moving.
Statement I is false. Particles keep moving at 0 °C because it is well above absolute zero.

q:
Which substances are strong electrolytes when dissolved in water?
I. Glucose, C6H12O6
II. Potassium bromide, KBr
III. Ethanol, C2H5OH
h: Soluble ionic compounds break apart into ions. Molecular compounds such as sugars and alcohols dissolve as whole molecules.
w: I is a nonelectrolyte: glucose dissolves as molecules, not ions. II is a strong electrolyte: KBr is a soluble ionic compound that separates completely into K+ and Br−. III is a nonelectrolyte: ethanol dissolves as molecules, and its OH group does not break off as OH−. The answer is II only.
x: Statement I is a nonelectrolyte. Glucose dissolves as whole molecules and makes no ions.
Statement III is a nonelectrolyte. The OH in ethanol is not a hydroxide ion and does not break off.
Statement I is a nonelectrolyte. A sugar dissolves as molecules, not ions.

q:
Which pairs of aqueous solutions form a precipitate when mixed?
I. KNO3 and NaCl
II. Na2CO3 and KCl
III. AgNO3 and NaCl
h: Swap the partners and check each new compound against the solubility rules. Compounds of Na⁺, K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are always soluble.
w: I: swapping gives KCl and NaNO3, both soluble, so no precipitate forms. II: swapping gives NaCl and K2CO3, both soluble (carbonates of Na+ and K+ dissolve). III: swapping gives insoluble AgCl plus NaNO3. Only III forms a precipitate.
x: Statement I forms no precipitate. KCl and NaNO₃ are both soluble.
Statement II forms no precipitate. Carbonates of sodium and potassium are soluble.
Statement II forms no precipitate. NaCl and K₂CO₃ both dissolve.

q:
For the reaction 2 H2(g) + O2(g) → 2 H2O(l), which statements are true?
I. 2 mol of H2 react with 1 mol of O2.
II. 1 mol of O2 produces 2 mol of H2O.
III. 2 g of H2 react with 1 g of O2.
h: Coefficients give mole ratios, not mass ratios. To compare grams, convert with molar masses.
w: I is true: the coefficients 2 and 1 give the mole ratio of H2 to O2. II is true: the mole ratio of O2 to H2O is 1 : 2. III is false: 2 g of H2 is about 1 mol, which needs about 0.5 mol (16 g) of O2, not 1 g. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II is true. The coefficients show that 1 mol of O₂ gives 2 mol of H₂O.
Statement III is false. Coefficients are mole ratios, and H₂ and O₂ have very different molar masses.
Statement III is false. Coefficients compare moles, not grams.

q:
Consider the reaction HCl(aq) + H2O(l) → H3O+(aq) + Cl−(aq). Which statements are true?
I. HCl acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
II. H2O acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base.
III. Cl− is the conjugate base of HCl.
h: An acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts it. A conjugate base is what is left after an acid loses H⁺.
w: I is true: HCl donates H+. II is true: H2O accepts that H+ and becomes H3O+. III is true: removing H+ from HCl leaves Cl−, its conjugate base. The answer is I, II and III.
x: Statement III is true. HCl minus one H⁺ is Cl⁻, which makes Cl⁻ its conjugate base.
Statement II is true. Water accepts an H⁺ and becomes H₃O⁺.
Statement II is true. Accepting H⁺ makes water the base in this reaction.

q:
Rank these solutions at 25 °C from lowest pH to highest pH.
I. A solution with [H3O+] = 0.001 M
II. A solution with [OH−] = 0.001 M
III. Pure water
h: A higher [H₃O⁺] means a lower pH. Pure water at 25 °C has pH 7, and pH + pOH = 14.
w: I: [H3O+] = 0.001 M, so pH = 3 (acidic). II: [OH−] = 0.001 M, so pOH = 3 and pH = 14 − 3 = 11 (basic). III: pure water has pH 7. Lowest to highest: I < III < II.
x: This order is reversed. A high [H₃O⁺] gives a low pH, so the acidic solution has the lowest pH.
Pure water (pH 7) is not the most acidic. A solution with extra H₃O⁺ has a lower pH than water.
Solution II is basic, not neutral. Extra OH⁻ makes its pH greater than 7.

q:
Which statements are true for any chemical reaction at equilibrium?
I. The forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates.
II. The concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
III. The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped.
h: Equilibrium is dynamic. Ask what stays the same and what is still happening.
w: I is true: at equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so the amounts stop changing. II is false: the concentrations stay constant, but they are usually not equal to each other. III is false: both reactions keep going (dynamic equilibrium) at the same rate. The answer is I only.
x: Statement II is false. Concentrations stay constant at equilibrium, but they need not be equal.
Statement III is false. Equilibrium is dynamic, so both reactions keep happening.
Statement I is true. Equal forward and reverse rates are what define equilibrium.

q:
A 40 mg sample of a radioisotope has a half-life of 6 hours. Which statements are true?
I. After 12 hours, none of the isotope remains.
II. Heating the sample shortens its half-life.
III. After 18 hours, 5 mg of the isotope remains.
h: Each half-life cuts the amount in half. Radioactive decay is not affected by temperature.
w: I is false: 12 hours is 2 half-lives, so 40 → 20 → 10 mg remains. II is false: a half-life does not depend on temperature. III is true: 18 hours is 3 half-lives, so 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 mg remains. The answer is III only.
x: Statement I is false. Two half-lives leave one quarter of the sample, not zero.
Statement II is false. Temperature does not change how fast a nucleus decays.
Statement I is false. Each half-life halves the amount, so the sample does not drop to zero.

q: A nurse records four observations about a patient. Which one is quantitative?
c: Heart rate is 88 beats per minute.
h: Look for the observation that has both a number and a unit.
w: A quantitative observation is a measurement: a number with a unit. Only 88 beats per minute fits. The other three describe qualities (temperature feel, odor, appearance) in words, so they are qualitative.
x: Warm and dry are descriptions in words with no number, so this is qualitative.
An odor described in words is qualitative; nothing was measured.
Cloudy is a quality you see, not a measured number with a unit, so it is qualitative.

q: A microbiology student incubates identical agar plates, each spread with the same sample of E. coli, at 25 °C, 30 °C and 37 °C. After 24 hours she counts the colonies on each plate. What is the independent variable?
c: The number of colonies on each plate
The type of agar in the plates
h: Ask: what did she deliberately change from plate to plate?
w: The independent variable is the one thing the experimenter deliberately changes: the incubation temperature. The colony count is the dependent variable (what she measured), and the time and agar type are constants kept the same for every plate.
x: The colony count is what she measured; it depends on the change she made.
Every plate was incubated for 24 hours, so time was kept constant.
All the plates used the same agar, so it was kept constant.

q: A Tulare County farmer wants to know whether a new compost increases pistachio yield. Which setup gives her a proper control?
c: A matching block that gets no compost but the same water, soil and care
A block of trees that gets twice as much of the new compost, with the same care
A block of trees in a different county with different soil and water
Weighing the nuts from the composted trees twice
h: A control is the trial where you leave out the one change you are testing.
w: A fair experiment compares a trial with the change to a trial without it, keeping everything else the same. A matching block with no compost is the control. A block in a different county changes several things at once, so the result could not be traced to the compost.
x: This changes the amount of compost, which is a second test condition, not a comparison without the change.
Changing the soil and water too means she could not tell which difference caused a change in yield.
Repeating a measurement checks the measurement but gives nothing to compare against.

q: Which statement about a scientific theory is correct?
c: It is a well-tested explanation of why something happens, and new evidence can revise it.
It is an explanation that turns into a law once enough experiments prove it true.
It is an educated guess about why something happens that has not been tested yet.
It is a summary of what always happens in nature, without explaining why it happens.
h: In science, which is stronger: a guess or an explanation supported by many experiments?
w: In science a theory is a well-tested explanation of why nature behaves as it does, supported by many experiments, and it can be revised by new evidence (as models of the atom were). It does not turn into a law, and it is not a guess.
x: Theories and laws do different jobs, why versus what. A theory never graduates into a law.
That is the everyday meaning of theory. In science, an untested idea is a hypothesis.
Describing what happens without saying why is the job of a law.

q: The box models a sample of water with some oxygen gas dissolved in it. How is the sample classified?
c: A mixture of an element and a compound
A mixture of two different compounds
h: Identify each kind of particle separately: does it contain one kind of atom or two?
w: The box holds two kinds of particles that are not bonded to each other, so it is a mixture. H2O molecules contain two elements (a compound) and O2 molecules contain one (an element): a mixture of an element and a compound. Every particle contains oxygen, but that does not make them the same substance.
x: A pure substance has only one kind of particle; this box has two.
O<sub>2</sub> contains only one kind of atom, so it is an element, not a compound.
Some particles contain two different kinds of atoms bonded together, so the sample is not just an element.

q: Which substance is an element?
h: Count the different element symbols in each formula, not the subscripts.
w: A formula with only one element symbol is an element, subscript or not, so O3 is an element. CO, H2O2 and NaCl each contain two different elements bonded together, so they are compounds.
x: C and O are two different elements bonded together, so CO is a compound.
H and O are two different elements bonded in a fixed ratio, so this is a compound.
Na and Cl are two different elements, so NaCl is a compound.

q: A clinical lab needs to separate the plasma from the blood cells in a blood sample quickly. Which method uses the difference in density between the parts?
h: Which method spins a sample so the denser parts settle?
w: Centrifugation spins the tube so the denser red blood cells pack at the bottom and the less dense plasma rises to the top. Separation methods work because the parts of a mixture are not bonded; each method uses a physical property (here, density).
x: Distillation uses differences in boiling point and would boil and damage the sample.
Filtration separates by particle size, and a coffee filter would not separate cells from plasma well.
Evaporation drives off the liquid, which would destroy the plasma rather than collect it.

q: Which method would best separate ethanol from water in a mixture of the two liquids?
h: The two liquids mix completely. What property differs between them?
w: Ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (100 °C) form a homogeneous mixture, so you cannot filter or pour them apart. Distillation uses the difference in boiling point: ethanol vaporizes first and is condensed and collected.
x: Filtration separates a solid from a liquid by particle size; both of these are dissolved liquids that pass through.
Decanting needs separate layers, but ethanol and water mix completely.
Neither ethanol nor water is attracted to a magnet.

q: Which statement about the particles in a solid, such as a piece of ice, is correct?
c: They do not move at all.
They are far apart from one another.
They slide freely past one another.
h: Solid particles are not frozen in time. What kind of motion can they still have?
w: The particles in a solid are packed closely and held in position, but they vibrate in place. They do not stop moving, and they do not slide past each other (that is a liquid).
x: Particles in a solid still have kinetic energy, so they are never completely still.
Solid particles are packed closely together, not far apart.
Sliding past one another describes a liquid, which is why liquids flow.

q: Which of these solids is amorphous rather than crystalline?
h: Crystalline solids have particles in a regular, repeating pattern. Which one has jumbled particles?
w: Glass is an amorphous solid: it holds its shape, but its particles are disordered. Table salt, ice and quartz are crystalline, with particles arranged in regular, repeating patterns.
x: Salt is made of ions in a regular repeating pattern, so it is crystalline.
Water molecules in ice sit in a regular repeating pattern, so ice is crystalline.
Quartz has a regular repeating arrangement of atoms, so it is crystalline.

q: Four pairs of ions are each held the same distance apart. Which pair attracts most strongly?
h: The distance is the same for every pair, so compare the sizes of the charges, and make sure the pair really attracts.
w: At the same distance, larger charges give a stronger force. Mg2+ and O2− have charges of 2+ and 2−, so they attract more strongly than the 1+/1− pairs. Ca2+ and Mg2+ are both positive, so they repel.
x: These are opposite charges, but only 1+ and 1−, smaller than another pair's.
These attract, but with charges of only 1+ and 1−.
Both ions are positive, so this pair repels rather than attracts.

q: A K<sup>+</sup> ion and an F<sup>−</sup> ion move from 4 nm apart to 1 nm apart. How does the force between them change?
c: The force changes from attraction to repulsion.
h: The charges did not change. What did change, and which way does that push the strength of the force?
w: The charges stay 1+ and 1−, so they still attract, but the distance shrank. Charges pull on each other more strongly when they are closer, so the attraction gets stronger.
x: The force weakens as charges move apart, not as they move closer.
Distance matters: the same two charges attract more strongly when they are closer.
The signs did not change (still + and −), so they still attract.

q: What must happen to pull a Na<sup>+</sup> ion and a Cl<sup>−</sup> ion farther apart?
c: Energy must be added, because the opposite charges attract each other.
Energy is released, because the ions want to separate from each other.
No energy is involved, because the ions are neutral.
Energy is released, because like charges repel.
h: Think of pulling two magnets apart that are stuck together.
w: Because opposite charges attract, separating them is like pulling two magnets apart: energy must be added. When opposite charges come together, energy is released. This is why breaking up an ionic solid takes energy.
x: Opposite charges pull toward each other; separating them costs energy rather than releasing it.
The ions are charged (+ and −), not neutral.
Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> have opposite charges, not like charges.

q: In a resting nerve cell, the inside of the membrane is slightly negative compared with the outside. When sodium channels open, Na<sup>+</sup> ions rush into the cell. Which idea best explains why?
c: Positive Na<sup>+</sup> ions are attracted to the negative interior.
Positive Na<sup>+</sup> ions are repelled by the negative interior.
Na<sup>+</sup> ions are neutral, so charge plays no role.
Like charges attract, so Na<sup>+</sup> moves toward other positive ions.
h: Compare the charge of Na<sup>+</sup> with the charge on the inside of the cell.
w: The Na+ ions are positive and the cell interior is negative, so opposite charges attract and pull the ions inward. Keeping the charges separated beforehand costs the cell energy, which it spends running ion pumps.
x: Repulsion happens between like charges; + and − attract.
Na<sup>+</sup> carries a 1+ charge; the plus sign shows it is an ion, not neutral.
Like charges repel; they do not attract.

q: In the catalase test, a microbiology student adds a drop of hydrogen peroxide to a bit of a bacterial colony and the drop bubbles vigorously as oxygen gas forms. What does the bubbling show?
c: A chemical change: peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen
A physical change: the peroxide is boiling
A physical change: the peroxide is evaporating
A physical change: oxygen was already dissolved and is escaping
h: Gas forming without boiling is one of the signs of a chemical change. What new substances form?
w: The bacterium's enzyme, catalase, breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas. New substances form, so the bubbling is a chemical change. Catalase-positive bacteria, such as Staphylococcus, bubble; bacteria without catalase do not.
x: Nothing was heated, and the gas is oxygen, a new substance, not peroxide vapor.
Evaporation would not make vigorous bubbles of a new gas, oxygen.
The oxygen is produced as the enzyme catalase breaks down peroxide; it was not simply dissolved there before.

q: Which of these properties of a silver ring is extensive?
h: An extensive property changes if you have more or less of the sample.
w: Extensive properties depend on the amount of sample: volume (and mass) would double for a ring twice as large. Melting point, color and density are intensive; they are the same for any amount, which makes them useful for identifying a substance.
x: Melting point is the same for a speck or a bar of silver, so it is intensive.
Color does not depend on the amount of silver, so it is intensive.
Density is a ratio that stays the same for a small or a large piece of silver, so it is intensive.

q: A lab note reads: “The acetone spilled on the bench evaporated within a few minutes.” How is this best classified?
h: First decide: property (a description) or change (an event)? Then: did a new substance form?
w: The note describes an event, so it is a change, and evaporation forms no new substance, so it is a physical change. “Acetone evaporates easily” would be a physical property; “acetone is flammable” would be a chemical property.
x: No new substance formed; evaporation only changes the state.
A property describes what a substance is or can do; this note describes an event that happened.
A property is not an event, and evaporation does not form a new substance.

q: A dental hygienist paints a liquid sealant onto a molar and shines a curing light on it. The light triggers a reaction that links the small molecules of the liquid into a hard, solid plastic that will not melt back into the original liquid. What kind of change is this?
c: Chemical, because new substances with different properties form
Physical, because the sealant only changed from liquid to solid
Physical, because light was the only thing added
Chemical, because every change from liquid to solid is chemical
h: Is the hardened sealant still the same substance as the liquid, just colder or in a new state?
w: The curing light starts a reaction that joins small molecules into a new, solid plastic that does not turn back into the liquid. New substances formed, so it is a chemical change, even though it looks like a liquid becoming a solid.
x: Freezing is physical, but here the molecules themselves were linked into new ones; it is not simple freezing.
Adding light does not make a change physical; what matters is whether new substances form.
Freezing water is liquid to solid and is physical, so this rule is not true.

q: The diagram shows nitrogen and hydrogen before and after a reaction that makes ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, a fertilizer widely used on Valley farms. Which statement is correct?
c: The atoms are rearranged into new molecules, and no atoms are gained or lost.
The atoms are rearranged into new molecules, and some nitrogen atoms are destroyed.
No new substance forms, so this is a physical change.
New atoms are created to build the ammonia molecules.
h: Count each kind of atom in the Before box and in the After box.
w: Before: 2 N2 + 6 H2 = 4 N and 12 H atoms. After: 4 NH3 = 4 N and 12 H atoms. In a chemical change atoms are rearranged into new substances, but none are created or destroyed; this is why mass is conserved.
x: Count the N atoms: 4 before (in 2 N<sub>2</sub>) and 4 after (in 4 NH<sub>3</sub>). None are destroyed.
NH<sub>3</sub> is a new substance that was not present before, so this is a chemical change.
Atoms are never created in a chemical change; the 12 H atoms after were all there before.

q: A 20.0 mL sample of an alcohol-based hand sanitizer has a mass of 17.4 g. What is its density?
h: Density = mass ÷ volume. Write the units in the fraction too.
w: d = m/V = 17.4 g ÷ 20.0 mL = 0.870 g/mL. Check: the mass in grams is less than the volume in mL, so the density should be less than 1 g/mL, and it is.
x: This is volume divided by mass (20.0 ÷ 17.4); the fraction is upside down.
This multiplies mass by volume; density divides mass by volume.
This is a decimal slip. 17.4 g in 20.0 mL is close to 1 g/mL, not 0.1 g/mL.

q:
A small fishing weight has a mass of 56.5 g and a volume of 5.00 cm3. Using the densities given, which metal is it most likely made of?
aluminum 2.70 g/cm3; steel about 7.9 g/cm3; lead 11.3 g/cm3; gold 19.3 g/cm3
h: Calculate d = m/V, then find the matching density in the list.
w: d = m/V = 56.5 g ÷ 5.00 cm3 = 11.3 g/cm3, lead. Because density is intensive, it works as an identifying property no matter how big the sample is.
x: Aluminum (2.70 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) is much less dense than the value you get from m/V here.
Steel (about 7.9 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) is less dense than this weight's calculated density.
Gold (19.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) is denser than this weight's calculated density.

q: A plastic cap has a mass of 4.60 g and a volume of 5.00 mL. Water has a density of 1.00 g/mL and ethanol 0.789 g/mL. What happens to the cap in each liquid?
c: It floats in water and sinks in ethanol.
It sinks in water and floats in ethanol.
h: Find the cap's density first, then compare it with each liquid's density.
w: d = 4.60 g ÷ 5.00 mL = 0.920 g/mL. It is less dense than water (1.00 g/mL), so it floats in water, and denser than ethanol (0.789 g/mL), so it sinks in ethanol.
x: This is reversed: an object floats only in a liquid denser than itself.
The cap is denser than ethanol, so it cannot float in ethanol.
The cap is less dense than water, so it floats in water.

q: Honey (1.42 g/mL), water (1.00 g/mL) and mineral oil (0.85 g/mL) are carefully poured into a tall cylinder and form three separate layers. What is the order of the layers from top to bottom?
h: Least dense on top, densest on the bottom.
w: Liquids that do not mix stack with the least dense on top: mineral oil (0.85), then water (1.00), then honey (1.42) on the bottom.
x: This is bottom to top; the densest liquid (honey) belongs at the bottom.
Water (1.00 g/mL) is denser than mineral oil (0.85 g/mL), so it cannot sit on top of the oil.
Honey is denser than water, so it sinks below the water rather than sitting above it.

q: Which unit is the SI base unit of mass?
h: One SI base unit is unusual because its name already includes a prefix.
w: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram. It is the only base unit whose name includes a prefix (kilo- = 1000), so 1 kg = 1000 g.
x: The gram is a common metric unit, but the SI chose the kilogram, not the gram, as its base unit of mass.
A milligram is a small metric unit derived from the gram; it is not a base unit.
The pound is a U.S. customary unit, not part of the SI.

q: The spores of the fungus that causes Valley fever (coccidioidomycosis) are only a few micrometers (µm) across. What does the prefix micro- (µ) mean?
h: Put the small prefixes in order: centi-, milli-, micro-, nano-. Each step after milli- is a factor of 1000.
w: Micro- (µ) = 10−6. The small prefixes go centi- (10−2), milli- (10−3), micro- (10−6), nano- (10−9). Clinical orders often write mcg for micrograms so the µ is not misread as m.
x: One-thousandth is milli- (m), as in millimeter; micro- is a thousand times smaller than milli-.
One-hundredth is centi- (c), as in centimeter.
One-billionth is nano- (n), as in nanometer; micro- is a thousand times larger than nano-.

q: Four samples of flour are weighed for a food-science lab. Which sample has the largest mass?
h: Convert every mass to grams before you compare.
w: In grams: 0.50 kg = 500 g; 455 g; 4.8 × 105 mg = 480 g; 5.2 × 104 cg = 520 g. The largest is 5.2 × 104 cg. A big number in front of a small unit can still be a small amount, so always compare in the same unit.
x: 0.50 kg is 500 g; it is large, but one of the other samples is 20 g more.
455 g is already in grams, and it is actually the smallest: the other three are 480 g, 500 g and 520 g once you convert them.
1 g = 1000 mg, so 4.8 × 10<sup>5</sup> mg is 480 g, which is not the largest.

q: A virus particle is about 1 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m across. Which length is about the same?
h: Write each choice as a power of ten in meters: nano- = 10<sup>−9</sup>, micro- = 10<sup>−6</sup>.
w: Nano- = 10−9, so 10−7 m = 102 × 10−9 m = 100 nm. Viruses are usually measured in nanometers; bacteria and cells in micrometers.
x: 10 nm is 10<sup>−8</sup> m, ten times smaller than the virus.
1 µm is 10<sup>−6</sup> m, ten times larger than the virus.
100 µm is 10<sup>−4</sup> m, about the width of a hair and a thousand times larger than the virus.

q: Which measurement has exactly two significant figures?
h: Trailing zeros count only when the number shows a decimal point.
w: 3800 mL has two significant figures: with no decimal point, its trailing zeros are placeholders. To show more precision, write 3800. mL (four) or 3.80 × 103 mL (three).
x: The decimal point after the zeros makes them significant, so this has four significant figures.
In scientific notation every digit in the coefficient counts, so 3.80 has three significant figures.
Leading zeros do not count, but the trailing zeros after the decimal point do, so this has four.

q: Which value has an unlimited number of significant figures?
c: 24.0 mL of cough syrup measured out
h: Exact numbers come from counting or from definitions. Which of these was counted?
w: Counted items are exact, so 24 tablets has unlimited significant figures and never limits a calculation. Defined equalities within one system (1 kg = 1000 g) and 1 in = 2.54 cm are exact too; rounded factors such as 1 lb = 453.59 g are not.
x: A volume read from glassware is a measurement, so it carries uncertainty and three significant figures.
A mass read from a scale is a measurement with uncertainty; it has two significant figures.
This equality is a rounded value (to five significant figures), so it is not exact, even though it is a conversion factor.

q: One acetaminophen tablet has a mass of 0.325 g. What is the total mass of 12 tablets (counted), reported to the correct number of significant figures?
h: Counted numbers are exact. How many significant figures does the measured mass have?
w: 12 × 0.325 g = 3.9 on the calculator. The 12 is exact, so the answer keeps the three significant figures of 0.325 g: 3.90 g (the zero is added to show the third significant figure).
x: This treats 12 as a measurement with two significant figures, but a count is exact and never limits the answer.
The calculator shows 3.9, and adding zeros claims four significant figures, more than 0.325 g supports.
This keeps only one significant figure, far less than the three in 0.325 g.

q: A pharmacy technician weighs a container (102 g, on a coarse scale), then adds 0.85 g and 1.236 g of two powders measured on an analytical balance. What is the total mass, to the correct precision?
h: For addition and subtraction, look at decimal places, not the number of significant figures.
w: 102 + 0.85 + 1.236 = 104.086 g. The least precise value, 102 g, is known only to the ones place, so round to the ones place: 104 g.
x: This keeps every calculator digit; the total cannot be more precise than the 102 g measured to the ones place.
This keeps two decimal places, but 102 g has no decimal places, so the ones place is the limit.
This applies the multiplication rule (fewest significant figures); addition uses decimal places instead.

q: A dental materials student finds the mass of a resin sample by difference (24.6 g − 22.1 g) and then divides by its volume, 1.335 mL. What density should she report?
h: Do the subtraction first and count the significant figures in that result before you divide.
w: Step 1 (subtraction, decimal-place rule): 24.6 g − 22.1 g = 2.5 g (tenths place, two significant figures). Step 2 (division): 2.5 g ÷ 1.335 mL = 1.8727… g/mL → two significant figures: 1.9 g/mL. Keep extra digits in the calculator between steps, but track the significant figures each step allows.
x: This keeps three significant figures, as if the mass still had three; after subtracting, 2.5 g has two.
This keeps four significant figures from the volume, ignoring the less precise mass.
This keeps only one significant figure; the mass (2.5 g) supports two.

q: A vitamin B<sub>12</sub> tablet contains 2.50 × 10<sup>2</sup> µg of the vitamin. What is that mass in grams?
h: Micro- = 10<sup>−6</sup>. Going to a bigger unit makes the number smaller.
w: 2.50 × 102 µg × (1 g / 106 µg) = 2.50 × 10−4 g. (That is 0.250 mg; orders write mcg for micrograms.)
x: This uses 1 g = 1000 µg, which is the factor for milligrams, not micrograms.
This multiplies by 10<sup>6</sup>; converting to a larger unit (grams) must give a smaller number.
This uses 10<sup>9</sup> per gram, the factor for nanograms, not micrograms.

q: A wound care nurse records a skin wound area of 6.0 cm<sup>2</sup>. What is the area in mm<sup>2</sup>? (1 cm = 10 mm)
h: 1 cm<sup>2</sup> is a square 10 mm on a side. How many mm<sup>2</sup> is that?
w: 6.0 cm2 × (10 mm / 1 cm)2 = 6.0 cm2 × 100 mm2/cm2 = 6.0 × 102 mm2. Scientific notation keeps the two significant figures clear.
x: This uses 10 mm/cm only once; an area unit is squared, so the factor must be squared too.
This divides by 100; a millimeter is smaller than a centimeter, so the number of mm<sup>2</sup> must be larger.
This cubes the factor (10<sup>3</sup>), which is right for volume, not for area.

q: A dairy's water storage tank holds 2.40 m<sup>3</sup>. How many liters is that? (1 m = 100 cm; 1 mL = 1 cm<sup>3</sup>)
h: Cube the length factor: (100 cm / 1 m)<sup>3</sup>. Then use 1 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1 mL.
w: 2.40 m3 × (100 cm / 1 m)3 = 2.40 × 106 cm3 = 2.40 × 106 mL; × (1 L / 1000 mL) = 2.40 × 103 L. (1 m3 = 1000 L.)
x: This uses the 100 cm/m factor only once; a cubic unit needs the factor cubed.
This stops at cubic centimeters (2.40 × 10<sup>6</sup> cm<sup>3</sup>) and calls them liters; a cubic centimeter is a milliliter.
This divides where it should multiply; a cubic meter is much larger than a liter, so there are many liters in it.

q: A Valley olive mill fills a 2.00 L bottle with olive oil (density 0.917 g/mL). What is the mass of the oil in kilograms?
h: Chain it: L → mL → g (density) → kg.
w: 2.00 L × (1000 mL / 1 L) × (0.917 g / 1 mL) × (1 kg / 1000 g) = 1.834 kg → 1.83 kg. Check: oil floats on water, so 2 L of oil should weigh a little less than 2 kg.
x: This stops at grams (1834 g) but labels the result kilograms; one more step, g → kg, is needed.
This divides by the density instead of multiplying, so the units cannot come out as mass.
The steps are right, but every given value has three significant figures, so the answer keeps three.

q: A nurse records a patient's 24-hour urine output as 1,800 mL, measured to three significant figures. How should it be written so that all three significant figures show?
h: Written as 1,800 with no decimal point, the number shows only 2 significant figures. In scientific notation, every digit in A counts.
w: Write A with exactly three digits: 1.80. The decimal point moved three places left, so the exponent is +3. Answer: 1.80 × 103 mL.
x: 1.8 shows only 2 significant figures, the same as writing 1,800 with no decimal point.
1.800 shows 4 significant figures, one more than was measured.
This has three significant figures, but 18.0 is not between 1 and 10, so it is not proper scientific notation.

q: A clinical laboratory scientist counts 3.6 × 10<sup>8</sup> bacteria in 9.0 × 10<sup>−1</sup> mL of a broth culture. How many bacteria are in each milliliter?
h: Divide the A parts and subtract the exponents, top minus bottom. Watch the sign of the bottom exponent.
w: 3.6 ÷ 9.0 = 0.40, and 8 − (−1) = 9: 0.40 × 109. Adjust A to be between 1 and 10: 4.0 × 108 bacteria/mL. Check: dividing by a number smaller than 1 makes the answer bigger than 3.6 × 108.
x: This subtracts 8 − 1 and ignores the minus sign on the −1. Subtracting a negative exponent adds: 8 − (−1) = 9.
Moving the decimal point of A to the right makes A bigger, so the exponent must go down by 1, not up.
This divides milliliters by bacteria (the factor is upside down). Bacteria per milliliter puts bacteria on top.

q: A lab reports a platelet count as 2.1 × 10<sup>11</sup> per liter. Which is the same count per microliter? (1 L = 10<sup>6</sup> µL) (Context only; reference ranges vary by laboratory.)
h: Is a microliter bigger or smaller than a liter? So should the count per microliter be bigger or smaller?
w: Divide by 106 µL per liter: subtract 6 from the exponent. 2.1 × 1011 ÷ 106 = 2.1 × 105 per µL (210,000 per microliter).
x: This adds 6 to the exponent. A microliter is much smaller than a liter, so the count per microliter must be smaller.
This uses 10<sup>3</sup>, the number of milliliters in a liter. That gives the count per milliliter, not per microliter.
This keeps the exponent and changes only the unit. Changing the unit changes the exponent: the same count per liter and per microliter differ by 10<sup>6</sup>.

q: A calculation of the number of yeast cells in a fermentation sample gives 2.0965 × 105 cells. Round it to three significant figures.
h: Round only A. Underline the third digit and look at the one digit to its right.
w: In A = 2.0965, underline the third digit, 9. The next digit is 6, so round up: 2.09 → 2.10. Bring the power of ten down unchanged: 2.10 × 105 cells.
x: This has only 2 significant figures. The zero after rounding up is significant and must be written.
This chops off the extra digits without rounding. The digit after the 9 is a 6, so round up.
This has 4 significant figures, one more than asked.

q: Context only; a math example. A pharmacy technician dissolves 2.45 g of a powder to make 50.0 mL of solution. What is the concentration in grams per milliliter, reported to the correct number of significant figures?
h: Grams per milliliter: which number goes on top? Then count significant figures in each measurement.
w: 2.45 g ÷ 50.0 mL = 0.049 g/mL on the calculator. Both values have 3 significant figures, so write 3: 0.0490 g/mL.
x: The calculator shows 0.049, but that has only 2 significant figures. Both measurements have 3, so add the significant zero.
This has 4 significant figures, one more than either measurement.
This divides milliliters by grams (50.0 ÷ 2.45), which is mL/g, not g/mL. Grams per milliliter puts grams on top.

q: A clinical lab technician mixes 0.75 g of one salt with 436 mg of another. What is the total mass in grams?
h: Can grams and milligrams be added directly? Convert first, then use the addition rule.
w: 436 mg × (1 g / 1000 mg) = 0.436 g. 0.75 g + 0.436 g = 1.186 g. Fewest decimal places is two (0.75): 1.19 g.
x: This keeps three decimal places, from 0.436 g. 0.75 g has only two, so it limits the answer.
This adds 436 and 0.75 as if they had the same unit. Milligrams must be converted to grams before adding.
This uses the multiplication rule (2 significant figures from 0.75). Adding uses decimal places.

q: Fresno has daily high temperatures of 104 °F, 101 °F, and 108 °F over three July days. What is the average high, reported to the correct number of significant figures?
h: Add first (top of the fraction), then divide. Is the 3 a measurement or a count?
w: (104 + 101 + 108) ÷ 3 = 313 ÷ 3 = 104.33. The sum has 3 significant figures and 3 is exact, so the average has 3: 104 °F.
x: This keeps a tenths digit. The readings and their sum are known only to the ones place, so the sum has 3 significant figures and so does the average.
This copies the calculator. Each temperature was recorded only to the ones place.
This treats the count 3 as a measurement with 1 significant figure. The number of days is exact.

q: A lab thermometer is marked every 1 °C. The top of the liquid column lines up exactly with the 37 °C mark. What temperature should you record?
h: Marks every 1 °C: which decimal place do you estimate? What is the estimate when the column is right on a mark?
w: The ones place is certain (37) and the tenths is estimated. Exactly on the mark means the estimate is 0: 37.0 °C.
x: This leaves out the estimated digit. Writing 37 °C says the thermometer was read only to the ones place.
This estimates two digits past the smallest mark. Only one is allowed.
The column is on the 37 mark, not halfway to 38.

q: A nurse sees a recorded volume of 2.35 mL for a liquid medication. Which tool could have given this reading? (Context only; always follow the order, the device instructions, and facility policy.)
c: An oral syringe marked every 0.1 mL
A medicine cup marked every 5 mL
A 100 mL graduated cylinder marked every 1 mL
A 50 mL cylinder marked every 1 mL
h: The last digit of a reading is the estimated one. How far apart must the marks be for the hundredths place to be estimated?
w: One estimated digit beyond the smallest mark: a reading to the hundredths needs marks every 0.1 mL. Answer: an oral syringe marked every 0.1 mL. Precision depends on the spacing of the marks, not the size of the tool.
x: Marks 5 mL apart allow an estimate only to about the ones place, not hundredths of a milliliter.
Marks every 1 mL give one decimal place (for example 2.4 mL), not two.
Marks every 1 mL give one decimal place, whatever the size of the cylinder.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. A clinical lab reports a child's blood lead level as 3.5 µg/dL. A research study lists results in mg/L. What is this result in mg/L? (1 dL = 10−1 L, so 10 dL = 1 L.)
h: Do the top (µg → g → mg) first, then the bottom (dL → L). A unit on the bottom cancels with a factor that has it on top.
w: 3.5 µg/dL × (1 g / 106 µg) × (1000 mg / 1 g) × (10 dL / 1 L) = 0.035 mg/L. All factors are exact; 3.5 has 2 significant figures. Check: ÷ 1000 for the top, × 10 for the bottom, so the number gets 100 times smaller.
x: Only the top unit was converted. µg/dL → mg/L also needs the bottom changed: a liter holds 10 deciliters, so multiply by 10.
The dL factor is upside down. dL is on the bottom of the given, so the next factor needs dL on top: 10 dL / 1 L.
The microgram factor went the wrong way. A milligram is bigger than a microgram, so the number of milligrams must be smaller.

q: An irrigation well on a Central Valley almond farm pumps 450 gal/min (two significant figures). What is this flow rate in liters per second? (1 gal = 3.785 L)
h: Top: gal → L. Bottom: min → s, with minutes on top of that factor so they cancel.
w: 450 gal/min × (3.785 L / 1 gal) × (1 min / 60 s) = 28.39 L/s → 28 L/s. 450 has 2 significant figures; 60 s = 1 min is exact. Check: one gallon a minute is a bit under 4 L a minute, and a second is 1/60 of a minute: 450 × 4 ÷ 60 ≈ 30.
x: The setup is right, but 450 (no decimal point) has only 2 significant figures, so the answer gets 2.
The gallon factor is upside down (dividing by 3.785). A liter is smaller than a gallon, so there must be more liters than gallons.
The time factor is upside down (multiplying by 60). Minutes are on the bottom, so the factor is 1 min / 60 s; the number per second must be smaller than the number per minute.

q: A lab technician has a protein stock solution at 8.5 g/L and needs its concentration in mg/mL. Which setup is correct?
h: Check each factor: is the unit you want to cancel on the opposite side of where it sits in the given?
w: g is on top, so use 1000 mg / 1 g; L is on the bottom, so use 1 L / 1000 mL: 8.5 g/L × (1000 mg / 1 g) × (1 L / 1000 mL) = 8.5 mg/mL. The two factors of 1000 cancel, so g/L and mg/mL are the same number.
x: The volume factor is upside down. L is on the bottom of the given, so the factor needs L on top; here L would be left as L<sup>2</sup> on the bottom.
The mass factor is upside down: g on top of the given needs g on the bottom of the factor. Here grams do not cancel at all.
Only the top unit was converted; this gives 8500 mg/L. A concentration needs both its top and its bottom unit changed.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. An IV pump delivers a drug at 0.80 mg/min. The pharmacy record lists the rate in micrograms per hour (mcg/h; mcg is the health-care symbol for µg). What is the rate in mcg/h?
h: Top: mg → g → mcg. Bottom: min → h, with minutes on top of that factor.
w: 0.80 mg/min × (1 g / 1000 mg) × (106 mcg / 1 g) × (60 min / 1 h) = 48,000 mcg/h = 4.8 × 104 mcg/h. Scientific notation shows the 2 significant figures of 0.80. Check: 800 mcg each minute for 60 minutes is about 50,000 mcg.
x: The time factor is upside down (dividing by 60). A pump delivers more in an hour than in a minute.
The mass factor went the wrong way (dividing by 1000). A microgram is smaller than a milligram, so there are more of them.
Only the top unit was converted: 800 mcg is the amount per minute. The bottom (min → h) must change too.

q: Context only; a math example. A unit-practice worksheet gives a child's body surface area as 8.4 × 103 cm2. Drug references list body surface area in m2. What is it in m2? (1 m = 100 cm)
h: Square the whole factor 1 m / 100 cm, number and unit.
w: 8.4 × 103 cm2 × (1 m / 100 cm)2 = 8.4 × 103 ÷ 104 = 0.84 m2 (2 significant figures). Check: an average adult is about 1.7 to 2.0 m2, so a child under 1 m2 makes sense.
x: The factor 1 m / 100 cm was not squared (dividing by 100 only). Area needs 100<sup>2</sup> = 10<sup>4</sup>.
The squared factor is upside down (multiplying by 10<sup>4</sup>). A square meter is much bigger than a square centimeter, so the number must get smaller.
The factor was cubed (10<sup>6</sup>). Area has two dimensions, so square it.

q: Context only; a math example. Older lab reports gave blood cell counts per cubic millimeter (mm3); most labs now report per microliter (µL). How many microliters equal 1 mm3? (1 mm = 0.1 cm; 1 cm3 = 1 mL)
h: Cube 0.1 cm to get mm<sup>3</sup> in cm<sup>3</sup> (= mL), then go mL → L → µL.
w: 1 mm3 × (0.1 cm / 1 mm)3 = 10−3 cm3 = 10−3 mL; 10−3 mL × (1 L / 1000 mL) × (106 µL / 1 L) = 1 µL. A platelet count of 250,000/mm3 is the same as 250,000/µL.
x: This uses 1 mm = 0.1 cm without cubing it (0.1 mL = 100 µL). The whole factor must be cubed.
This squares the factor (0.01 mL = 10 µL). A volume needs the cube.
This stops at 0.001 mL and writes µL. One more step is needed: 0.001 mL × (1000 µL / 1 mL).

q: Aluminum has a density of 2.70 g/cm<sup>3</sup>. Engineers often list densities in kg/m<sup>3</sup>. What is the density of aluminum in kg/m<sup>3</sup>?
h: Do the top (g → kg) and the bottom (cm<sup>3</sup> → m<sup>3</sup>) separately. Cube the whole length factor.
w: 2.70 g/cm3 × (1 kg / 1000 g) × (100 cm / 1 m)3 = 2.70 × 103 kg/m3 (3 significant figures; the factors are exact). Check: a cubic meter of aluminum is a big block, so 2700 kg (about 3 tons) is reasonable.
x: The factor 100 cm / 1 m was not cubed (× 100 instead of × 10<sup>6</sup>), so cm<sup>3</sup> does not cancel.
The bottom was converted, but the top was left in grams. Change g → kg too.
The cubed factor is upside down. cm<sup>3</sup> is on the bottom of the given, so the factor needs cm<sup>3</sup> on top: (100 cm / 1 m)<sup>3</sup>.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. An order calls for 0.75 g of a drug. Each tablet on hand contains 250 mg. How many tablets make up the ordered amount?
h: The order is in grams and the label is in milligrams. Bridge them first.
w: 0.75 g × (1000 mg / 1 g) × (1 tablet / 250 mg) = 3.0 tablets (2 significant figures, from 0.75 g). Check: 0.75 g is 750 mg, three times 250 mg.
x: The grams were never converted to milligrams, so 0.75 was divided by 250 directly. The order and the label must be in the same unit first.
This uses 100 mg = 1 g. Milli- means one-thousandth: 1 g = 1000 mg.
The tablet factor is upside down (250 ÷ 0.75). Start with the order, then put mg on the bottom of the tablet factor.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. An order calls for 375 mg of an antibiotic. The oral suspension on hand is labeled 250. mg per 5.00 mL. What volume holds the ordered amount?
h: Start with the order. Which way up must the label factor be so mg cancels?
w: 375 mg × (5.00 mL / 250. mg) = 7.50 mL. Check: 375 mg is 1.5 times 250 mg, so the volume is 1.5 × 5 mL = 7.5 mL.
x: This divides 375 by 250 and stops; 1.50 is the number of 5.00 mL portions, not milliliters. Multiply by 5.00 mL.
The setup started with the label instead of the order (250 × 5.00 ÷ 375). Start with the term that stands alone, the order.
The label factor is upside down, so mg does not cancel. Put mg on the bottom: 5.00 mL / 250. mg.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. A patient who weighs 165 lb has an order for 2.5 mg/kg of a drug, twice a day. A vial contains 1.00 g of the drug. How many days will the vial last? (1 kg = 2.2046 lb)
h: Two quantities stand alone (the weight and the vial). Use the weight to build mg per day, then use that factor with the vial.
w: Part 1: 165 lb × (1 kg / 2.2046 lb) × (2.5 mg / 1 kg · dose) × (2 doses / 1 day) = 374.2 mg/day (do not round yet). Part 2: 1.00 g × (1000 mg / 1 g) × (1 day / 374.2 mg) = 2.67 days → 2.7 days.
x: This forgets “twice a day”; 5.3 is the number of doses, not days.
The pounds were used as if they were kilograms. Convert 165 lb to kg before using the per-kg order.
The pound factor is upside down (multiplying by 2.2046), which makes the patient seem to weigh 364 kg.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. A nurse is to infuse 600. mL of IV fluid over 5.00 h by gravity. The tubing delivers 10 drops per mL (a defined tubing calibration, exact). What drip rate, in drops per minute, is needed?
h: Write the rate 600. mL / 5.00 h, then change the bottom to minutes and the top to drops.
w: (600. mL / 5.00 h) × (1 h / 60 min) × (10 drops / 1 mL) = 20.0 drops/min (3 significant figures; 60 and 10 are exact). Check: 120 mL each hour is 2 mL each minute, and 2 mL is 20 drops.
x: The hours were never converted to minutes; 1200 is the number of drops per hour.
The drop factor is upside down (dividing by 10). mL is on top of the rate, so the factor needs mL on the bottom: 10 drops / 1 mL.
This stops at 2.00 mL/min. One more factor, 10 drops / 1 mL, turns milliliters into drops.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. An order reads 5.0 mcg/kg/min (micrograms per kilogram of body weight per minute) for a patient who weighs 80.0 kg. The pump is programmed in mg/h. What rate does the order describe, in mg/h?
h: Start with the weight. Then mcg → mg on top and min → h on the bottom.
w: 80.0 kg × (5.0 mcg / 1 kg·min) × (60 min / 1 h) × (1 mg / 1000 mcg) = 24 mg/h. Check: 400 mcg a minute is 0.4 mg a minute, and 0.4 × 60 = 24.
x: This stops at mg per minute. Multiply by 60 min / 1 h to get per hour.
The body weight was left out. The order is per kg, so it must be multiplied by the patient's 80.0 kg.
The mcg factor is upside down (multiplying by 1000). A milligram is larger than a microgram, so the number must get smaller.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. Normal saline is 0.90% sodium chloride, meaning 0.90 g of NaCl in every 100 mL of solution. How many grams of NaCl are in a 1.00 L IV bag of normal saline?
h: Write 0.90% as a fraction over 100 mL with both units labeled, then start with the bag volume.
w: 1.00 L × (1000 mL / 1 L) × (0.90 g NaCl / 100 mL solution) = 9.0 g NaCl. Check: 1 L is ten 100 mL portions, and 10 × 0.90 g = 9.0 g.
x: The liters were never converted to milliliters, so L did not cancel the mL in the percent factor.
This multiplies by 0.90 as a plain number. The percent factor is 0.90 g / 100 mL; leaving out the 100 makes the answer 100 times too big.
The percent factor is upside down (100 mL / 0.90 g), so mL does not cancel and the units come out wrong.

q: 14-karat gold is 58.3% gold by mass. A jeweler has 35.0 g of pure gold. What is the largest mass of 14-karat gold she can make with it?
h: Is 35.0 g the part or the total? Then which way up must the percent factor be?
w: 35.0 g gold × (100 g 14-karat gold / 58.3 g gold) = 60.03 g → 60.0 g (3 significant figures). Check: gold is a bit more than half the alloy, so the alloy is a bit less than twice 35 g.
x: The factor was not flipped: this finds 58.3% of 35.0 g. The total must come out larger than the part.
This multiplies by 58.3 as a plain number, leaving out the 100.
This uses 41.7% (the other metals) instead of 58.3% gold. The gold is the part that is given, so use the gold percent.

q: A student evaporates all the water from a 45.0 g sample of salt water and recovers 1.62 g of salt. What is the mass percent of salt in the sample?
h: Part ÷ total × 100%. Which mass is the whole sample?
w: % salt = (1.62 g salt / 45.0 g sample) × 100% = 3.60% (3 significant figures). Check: seawater is about 3.5% dissolved salts, so this is close to seawater.
x: This divides by the mass of the water (45.0 − 1.62 = 43.38 g), the other part, instead of by the total sample.
This is the decimal (0.0360) with a % sign added. Multiply by 100 to get a percent.
The fraction is upside down (total ÷ part). A part can never be more than 100% of its whole.

q: A soil sample from a Central Valley field is 42.5% sand and 38.0% silt by mass; the rest is clay. What mass of clay is in 250. g of this soil?
h: The parts of a whole add to 100%. What percent is left for clay?
w: Clay = 100% − 42.5% − 38.0% = 19.5%. 250. g soil × (19.5 g clay / 100 g soil) = 48.75 g → 48.8 g clay (3 significant figures). Check: about a fifth of 250 g is 50 g.
x: This is the mass of sand (42.5%). The question asks for the clay, the part left over.
This is the mass of silt (38.0%). Find the clay percent first: 100% minus the other two.
This multiplies by 19.5 as a plain number, leaving out the 100.

q: Which statement is part of Dalton's atomic theory?
c: Atoms of different elements combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
Every atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus.
Atoms contain negatively charged particles that can be pulled out by a high voltage.
In a chemical reaction, atoms of one element can turn into atoms of another element.
h: Dalton worked in the early 1800s, before anyone knew atoms had smaller parts.
w: Dalton's theory (early 1800s) says elements are made of atoms, atoms of one element are alike, atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed in reactions, and atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds. Electrons (Thomson) and the nucleus (Rutherford) came later.
x: The nucleus came from Rutherford's gold foil experiment about a century after Dalton; Dalton pictured atoms as solid, uncuttable spheres.
Charged particles inside atoms (electrons) were found by Thomson in 1897; Dalton's atoms had no smaller parts.
Dalton said the opposite: in a reaction atoms are only rearranged; they are never changed into atoms of a different element.

q: In a cathode-ray tube, the glowing beam bends toward a positively charged plate. What did Thomson conclude from this?
c: The beam is made of negatively charged particles.
The beam is made of positively charged particles.
The atom has a small, dense nucleus.
h: Recall the charge rules: opposite charges attract, like charges repel.
w: Opposite charges attract. A beam that bends toward the positive plate is negatively charged. Thomson showed the particles were the same for every metal he used: he had found the electron.
x: Like charges repel, so a positive beam would bend away from the + plate, not toward it.
A beam with no charge would not be pushed or pulled by a charged plate at all; it would go straight.
The nucleus was discovered later, with alpha particles and gold foil, not with cathode rays.

q: In the gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What does this observation show?
c: Most of the volume of an atom is empty space.
The nucleus fills most of the atom's volume.
Gold atoms have almost no mass.
h: Think about what an alpha particle would have to do to get through the foil without being turned.
w: Passing straight through means the alpha particles met nothing. So an atom is mostly empty space. The few that bounced back revealed the tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
x: A nucleus that filled the atom would sit in the path of nearly every alpha particle and turn many of them aside.
Alpha particles are positively charged; the result is about what they did or did not run into, not about their charge.
Gold is a heavy element; a few alpha particles even bounced back, which needs a lot of mass packed in one place.

q: Calcium carbonate, the active ingredient in many chewable antacids, is always 40.0% calcium by mass, whatever its source. How many grams of calcium are in a 1.25 g sample of pure calcium carbonate?
h: Change the percent to a decimal, then multiply by the mass of the sample.
w: By the law of definite proportions, every sample of calcium carbonate is 40.0% calcium. 1.25 g × 0.400 = 0.500 g of calcium. Check: the part (0.500 g) is smaller than the whole (1.25 g).
x: This divides by 0.400 instead of multiplying. The calcium must be less than the 1.25 g of compound it is part of.
This multiplies by 40.0 instead of 0.400. A percent must be divided by 100 before you use it.
This is 60.0% of the sample: the mass of the carbon and oxygen, not the calcium.

q: Which part of Dalton's atomic theory was later shown to be not quite right, once isotopes were discovered?
c: All atoms of a given element have the same mass.
Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, in chemical reactions.
Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
Each element is made of tiny particles called atoms.
h: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that differ in the number of neutrons. Which of Dalton's ideas does that contradict?
w: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so atoms of the same element do not all have the same mass. Dalton's other main ideas have held up.
x: This idea still holds; it is why mass is conserved in a chemical reaction.
This idea still holds; it is why every compound has a fixed composition.
This central idea still holds; it is the base of all of modern chemistry.

q: The atomic number (Z) of an element is the number of
c: protons in each of its atoms
neutrons in each of its atoms
protons plus neutrons in each of its atoms
electrons in every ion of the element
h: Which particle count can never change without the atom becoming a different element?
w: Z = number of protons. Every atom of an element has the same Z. A neutral atom also has Z electrons, but ions do not.
x: The number of neutrons can differ among atoms of the same element, so it cannot define the element.
Protons plus neutrons is the mass number (A), not the atomic number.
Ions have gained or lost electrons, so their electron count differs from Z; only a neutral atom has Z electrons.

q: A neutral atom has 53 electrons. The thyroid gland needs this element to make its hormones. Which element is it?
c: It cannot be identified without the mass number.
h: In a neutral atom, electrons = protons, and protons give the atomic number.
w: Neutral, so protons = electrons = 53. Z = 53 is iodine, I. The mass number tells you which isotope, but not which element.
x: Xenon has Z = 54, one more proton than this atom has.
Tellurium has Z = 52, one fewer proton than this atom has.
The identity depends only on the number of protons, and for a neutral atom that equals the number of electrons.

q: The diagram shows every particle in one atom. Which element is it, and is it neutral?
h: Count only the + particles to find the element. Then compare protons with electrons.
w: Nucleus: 9 protons and 10 neutrons. Outside: 9 electrons. Z = 9 is fluorine, and 9 protons with 9 electrons make it neutral. The fluoride ion in toothpaste would have one extra electron.
x: 19 is the total of protons and neutrons in the nucleus; the element is set by the protons alone.
10 is the number of neutrons; the element is set by the protons, not the neutrons.
An ion has unequal numbers of protons and electrons; count the two boxes again.

q: The atomic mass unit (amu) is defined as
c: one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
the mass of one hydrogen molecule, H<sub>2</sub>
h: The unit is tied to one particular isotope of carbon.
w: 1 amu = 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom = 1.6605 × 10−24 g. On this scale protons and neutrons are each about 1 amu.
x: An electron is about 0.00055 amu, far smaller than the unit.
A hydrogen molecule (H<sub>2</sub>) has a mass of about 2 amu, not 1.
A gram is enormous on the atomic scale: 1 amu is only about 1.6605 × 10<sup>−24</sup> g.

q: A respiratory therapy chart lists inhaled “NO” as a gas used for some newborns. What does NO stand for?
c: A compound of nitrogen and oxygen
h: A second letter in an element symbol is always lowercase.
w: A symbol has one capital letter, so NO is two symbols, N and O: the compound nitric oxide. Compare No (nobelium) and CO (carbon monoxide) with Co (cobalt).
x: Nobelium's symbol is No, with a lowercase o; NO with two capitals is two elements.
Sodium's symbol is Na, from the Latin natrium.
Neon’s symbol is Ne, with a lowercase e. NO has two capital letters, so it is two elements.

q: Calcium in bones and teeth is in group 2, period 4. The element marked X sits in the same group but one period higher. Which element is X?
h: Groups are columns; periods are rows numbered from the top.
w: Same group (column 2), one period higher (row 3): X is magnesium, Mg, another alkaline earth metal. Moving up or down a column keeps the group; moving across a row keeps the period.
x: Strontium is one period lower (period 5), not higher.
Potassium is in the same period as calcium but in group 1, one column to the left.
X is in a different row, so it cannot be calcium itself.

q: Dental amalgam fillings contain silver, tin, copper and mercury. Which list gives the correct symbols, in that order?
h: All four of these elements have symbols from Latin names.
w: Silver Ag (argentum), tin Sn (stannum), copper Cu (cuprum), mercury Hg (hydrargyrum). Ti is titanium, Si silicon and Co cobalt.
x: Ti is titanium, not tin; tin's symbol comes from the Latin stannum.
Si is silicon, a metalloid; silver's symbol comes from the Latin argentum.
Co is cobalt; copper's symbol comes from the Latin cuprum.

q: Which element is a nonmetal that is a liquid at room temperature?
h: Two elements are liquids at room temperature: one metal and one nonmetal.
w: Bromine is the one liquid nonmetal; mercury is the one liquid metal. Chlorine is a gas and iodine a solid, though all three halogens are nonmetals.
x: Mercury is a liquid, but it is a metal; it is the only metal that is not a solid at room temperature.
Chlorine is a nonmetal, but it is a gas at room temperature.
Iodine is a nonmetal, but it is a solid at room temperature.

q: Barium sulfate is a contrast medium that makes the digestive tract show up on X-ray images. Barium (Ba) is in group 2. Which family does it belong to?
h: Match the group number with the family name.
w: Group 2 is the alkaline earth metals: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba. Barium is a heavy atom, so it blocks X-rays well; calcium in the same family is in your bones.
x: Alkali metals are group 1 (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs).
Halogens are group 17 nonmetals (F, Cl, Br, I).
Transition metals fill groups 3–12 in the middle of the table.

q: A cation forms when a neutral atom
h: Charge = protons − electrons. What change makes that positive?
w: A cation is positive, so protons must outnumber electrons. That happens when the atom loses electrons. Metals usually form cations.
x: Gaining electrons makes the particle negative: that forms an anion.
Ions form by changing electrons only; changing the protons would make a different element.
Neutrons have no charge, so losing them cannot make an ion.

q: Many enzymes in the body hold a zinc ion, Zn<sup>2+</sup>. How many protons and electrons does Zn<sup>2+</sup> have?
h: Electrons = protons − charge.
w: Zn: Z = 30, so 30 protons. 2+ means two electrons lost: 30 − 2 = 28 electrons. Check: 30 − 28 = +2.
x: Adding electrons makes an ion more negative; a 2+ ion has fewer electrons than protons.
Ions form by losing electrons only; 28 protons would be nickel, not zinc.
30 electrons is the neutral atom; the 2+ charge means some were lost.

q: Predict the usual ion formed by phosphorus, and name it.
h: Find phosphorus's group. Nonmetals gain electrons, and their anions end in -ide.
w: Phosphorus is in group 15, so it has 5 valence electrons. Gaining 3 more gives it a full octet, like argon, so it forms P3−. A simple anion keeps the element’s root and ends in -ide: phosphide.
x: A nonmetal in group 15 gains electrons, so the charge is negative, not positive.
Group 15 does not form 5+ ions; it gains three electrons.
The charge is right, but anions are not named with the element name; they take -ide.

q: Iron supplements and hemoglobin involve the ions Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup>. How do these two ions differ?
c: Fe<sup>3+</sup> has one fewer electron than Fe<sup>2+</sup>.
Fe<sup>3+</sup> has one more proton than Fe<sup>2+</sup>.
Fe<sup>3+</sup> has one more electron than Fe<sup>2+</sup>.
Fe<sup>3+</sup> has one more neutron than Fe<sup>2+</sup>.
h: Charge = protons − electrons, and the protons are fixed for iron.
w: Both ions have 26 protons. Fe2+ has 26 − 2 = 24 electrons; Fe3+ has 26 − 3 = 23. The more positive ion has one fewer electron.
x: An extra proton would make a different element (cobalt); both ions are iron.
Gaining an electron would make the ion less positive, not more.
Neutrons have no charge, so they cannot change the ion's charge.

q: The mass number (A) of an atom is the number of
c: protons plus neutrons in its nucleus
protons, neutrons and electrons in the atom
h: A counts the heavy particles.
w: The mass number counts the particles in the nucleus: A = protons + neutrons. Electrons are too light to count. So neutrons = A − Z.
x: The number of protons alone is the atomic number, Z.
Neutrons alone are A − Z, not A.
Electrons are left out because they are so light.

q: Iodine-123 and iodine-131 are both used in thyroid studies. How many more neutrons does an iodine-131 atom have than an iodine-123 atom?
h: Same element means same protons. Where does the difference in mass number come from?
w: Iodine-123 has 123 − 53 = 70 neutrons; iodine-131 has 131 − 53 = 78. The difference is 8 neutrons, the same as 131 − 123.
x: They are the same element, so they have the same protons, but their mass numbers differ, so their neutrons differ.
78 is the number of neutrons in iodine-131 alone, not the difference.
70 is the number of neutrons in iodine-123 alone, not the difference.

q: The diagram shows the particles in one atom used in the urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori, a stomach bacterium. Which isotope is it?
h: Count the protons for the element. Add protons and neutrons for the mass number.
w: Nucleus: 6 protons and 7 neutrons, with 6 electrons outside. Z = 6 is carbon and A = 6 + 7 = 13: carbon-13, a stable isotope. Bacterial urease releases it as CO2 that the patient breathes out.
x: 7 is the neutron count; the element is set by the 6 protons.
The mass number counts protons and neutrons together, not neutrons alone.
13 is the mass number; Z = 13 would need 13 protons, and the nucleus has 6.

q: The thyroid absorbs radioactive iodine-131 just as it absorbs stable iodine-127. Why can't the gland tell them apart?
c: Both have the same number of protons and electrons, so they react the same way.
Both have the same number of neutrons.
Radioactive atoms are attracted to the thyroid gland by the radiation they give off.
h: What do isotopes of one element have in common, and which particles control chemical behavior?
w: Chemistry depends on electrons, and isotopes of iodine all have 53 protons and 53 electrons. So the thyroid takes up iodine-131 like iodine-127, which is what makes radioactive iodine useful in thyroid imaging and therapy.
x: Iodine-131 is about 4 amu heavier than iodine-127; the difference is in mass, not chemistry.
They have different numbers of neutrons (78 and 74); that is what makes them different isotopes.
Radiation does not attract the gland; the gland takes up iodine of any isotope because they react the same way.

q: A student calculates the average atomic mass of copper from its two isotopes (62.93 amu and 64.93 amu) and gets 6355 amu. What is the most likely mistake?
c: Multiplying by percent abundances instead of fractional abundances
Taking a simple average of the two masses instead of a weighted average
Swapping the abundances of the two isotopes
h: The average must fall between 62.93 and 64.93 amu. How far off is 6355?
w: Any average must lie between the isotope masses. 6355 is 100 times too big, the sign of using percents (69.15, 30.85) instead of fractions (0.6915, 0.3085). The correct answer is 63.55 amu.
x: A simple average would give 63.93 amu, which is still between the two masses.
Swapping abundances would give an answer near 64.3 amu, still between the two masses.
Early rounding changes the last digit or two, not the size of the answer by a factor of 100.

q: An element has two isotopes with masses 20.0 amu and 22.0 amu. Which value could be its average atomic mass?
h: Where must a weighted average fall?
w: Any weighted average lies between 20.0 and 22.0 amu, so only 20.2 amu is possible. It would mean the lighter isotope is far more abundant.
x: An average cannot be smaller than the lightest isotope.
An average cannot be larger than the heaviest isotope.
This adds the two masses; an average lies between them.

q: Carbon's average atomic mass is 12.011 amu. Which statement about a single carbon atom in a breath sample is true?
c: Its mass is close to 12.000 or 13.003 amu, depending on its isotope.
Its mass is exactly 12.011 amu, like every carbon atom.
It is most likely carbon-13, since the average of 12.011 is more than 12.
h: Is the average a property of one atom or of a large mixture of atoms?
w: The 12.011 amu value is an average over a mixture that is about 99% carbon-12 and 1% carbon-13. Any one atom has the mass of its own isotope: about 12.000 or 13.003 amu.
x: The average describes the mixture of isotopes; individual atoms have the mass of their own isotope.
Every atom has a whole number of neutrons (6 for carbon-12, 7 for carbon-13).
12.011 is only a little above 12, which shows that carbon-12 is by far the more common isotope (about 99%).

q: Light of one color is replaced by light whose wavelength is twice as long. What happens to the frequency?
c: It stays the same, because the speed of light does not change.
h: The product of wavelength and frequency is always the speed of light.
w: Because λν = c is constant, doubling λ means ν is cut in half. Longer waves pass a point less often.
x: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related; they cannot both go up while their product stays equal to c.
The speed stays the same, and that is exactly why the frequency has to change when the wavelength does.
Frequency changes by the same factor as the wavelength (2), only in the opposite direction; nothing is squared in c = λν.

q: Newborn jaundice is often treated with phototherapy, blue light that the baby's skin absorbs. One phototherapy lamp uses LEDs that give off light at 455 nm. What is the energy of one photon of this light? (h = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J·s; c = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s)
h: Convert nm to m, then either find ν first or use the combined equation E = hc/λ.
w: λ = 4.55 × 10−7 m. E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10−34)(3.00 × 108)/(4.55 × 10−7) = 4.37 × 10−19 J. This is context only: the energy of one photon, not a dose.
x: This leaves the wavelength in nanometers, so the energy is a billion (10<sup>9</sup>) times too small.
This is the frequency, c/λ, with joules written after it. One more step, E = hν, turns the frequency into an energy.
This divides h by λ and leaves out the speed of light. The combined equation is E = hc/λ.

q: A pulse oximeter shines red light at 660 nm and infrared light at 940 nm through a fingertip. Which statement compares the two photons correctly?
c: The 660 nm photon has the higher frequency and the higher energy.
The 940 nm photon has the higher energy, because its wavelength is larger.
The 940 nm photon has the higher frequency, but the 660 nm photon has the higher energy.
Both photons have the same energy, because both travel at the speed of light.
h: Wavelength goes one way; frequency and energy go the other way together.
w: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency (c = λν) and higher energy (E = hν). The 660 nm red photon has the higher frequency and energy, about 940/660 ≈ 1.4 times that of the infrared photon.
x: Energy and wavelength are inversely related: the longer 940 nm wave has less energy per photon.
Frequency and energy always go together (E = hν); a photon cannot have the higher frequency and the lower energy.
Every photon travels at c, but its energy depends on its frequency, and these frequencies differ.

q: A dental assistant turns a curing light to a brighter setting without changing its color. What changes?
c: More photons leave each second, each with the same energy.
Each photon now carries more energy than before.
The wavelength of each photon gets shorter.
The frequency of the light rises, so each photon is stronger.
h: What sets the energy of a single photon? Did that quantity change?
w: A brighter light sends out more photons, but each photon's energy depends only on its wavelength (E = hc/λ), which is unchanged because the color is the same.
x: The energy of a single photon is set by its wavelength, E = hc/λ, and a brighter setting does not change the color.
Changing the wavelength would change the color; the color stayed the same.
A higher frequency would mean a shorter wavelength and a different color, but the color stayed the same.

q: Radiology staff wear dosimeters and lead aprons around X-ray equipment, but nobody worries about the radio waves from a cell phone in the same way. Why?
c: An X-ray photon can knock electrons out of atoms; a radio photon has far too little energy.
X-rays travel faster than radio waves.
Radio waves have shorter wavelengths, so they pass through the body without stopping.
Radio waves are not electromagnetic radiation.
h: Compare the energy of one photon in each region.
w: X-rays and gamma rays are called ionizing radiation because each photon carries enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms. Radio photons have very long wavelengths and very low energies, too little to break bonds or ionize atoms.
x: All electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed, c.
Radio waves have the longest wavelengths in the spectrum, and long wavelength means low energy.
Radio waves are electromagnetic radiation, at the long-wavelength, low-energy end of the spectrum.

q: A UV-C germicidal lamp gives off light at 254 nm, and a sodium lamp gives off light at 589 nm. About how many times more energy does one UV-C photon carry than one sodium-lamp photon?
h: Write E = hc/λ for each photon and divide one by the other. What cancels?
w: EUV/ENa = (hc/254 nm)/(hc/589 nm) = 589/254 = 2.32. Shorter wavelength, more energy: each UV-C photon carries a bit more than twice the energy, enough to damage the DNA of microbes.
x: This is 254/589, the ratio the wrong way up; it says the UV-C photon has less energy, but its shorter wavelength means it has more.
This subtracts the wavelengths. A ratio of energies needs division, and the answer has no units of nm.
This squares the wavelength ratio. Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength itself, not to its square.
