q: White light from a bulb passes through a prism and spreads into a smooth rainbow. Light from a hydrogen discharge tube shows only a few sharp colored lines. What are these two kinds of spectra called?
c: The rainbow is a continuous spectrum; the hydrogen lines are a line spectrum.
The rainbow is a line spectrum; the hydrogen lines are a continuous spectrum.
Both are continuous spectra, because both come from light.
Both are emission spectra, so they always look the same.
h: Continuous means no gaps.
w: White light gives a continuous spectrum, every color with no gaps. A glowing gas such as hydrogen gives a line (emission) spectrum: only certain wavelengths, a pattern unique to that element.
x: This swaps the names: the smooth rainbow with no gaps is the continuous one.
The hydrogen tube gives only a few colors with dark gaps between them, so its spectrum is not continuous.
They look very different: one has every color, the other only a few lines. Each element's line spectrum is its own pattern.

q: In a hydrogen atom, which electron jump gives off the photon with the most energy?
h: Light is given off only when the electron drops to a lower level. Then compare the gaps: hydrogen’s levels get closer together as n gets larger.
w: A photon is given off only when the electron drops (n = 1 to n = 3 is a jump up, so it absorbs light). Among the three drops, the photon energy equals the gap between the levels, and hydrogen’s levels crowd together as n increases: the gap from n = 3 to n = 1 is about 0.89 of the full ionization energy, n = 4 to n = 2 about 0.19, and n = 5 to n = 3 about 0.07. So n = 3 to n = 1 gives the most energetic photon (an ultraviolet line); n = 4 to n = 2 gives hydrogen’s blue-green visible line.
x: This drop does give off light, but hydrogen’s levels get closer together as n increases, so the gap between n = 4 and n = 2 is small compared with a drop that ends at n = 1.
Moving up from n = 1 to n = 3 needs energy: the atom absorbs a photon here; it does not give one off.
This drop gives off light, but n = 3 and n = 5 are high levels that sit close together, so this is the smallest gap of the three drops.

q: A flame test turns a flame bright yellow-orange for sodium, red for strontium, and blue-green for copper. What does the Bohr model say causes each element's own colors?
c: Each element has its own fixed energy levels, so its electrons give off only certain wavelengths.
Each element absorbs every wavelength equally and then gives off the leftover colors.
The color depends only on how hot the flame is, not on which element is in it.
Electrons can have any energy, so each element just favors one color of light.
h: Think about the staircase picture: which steps does each element have?
w: Heat excites the electrons; when they drop back, each drop releases a photon whose energy equals the gap. Because each element has its own fixed energy levels, it gives off its own set of wavelengths, like a bar code.
x: The colors come from electrons dropping between that element's own levels, not from leftovers of absorbed light.
The same flame gives different colors for different elements, so the element, not just the heat, sets the color.
In the Bohr model electron energies are quantized: only certain values are allowed, with nothing in between.

q: Which statement describes an atom in an excited state?
c: At least one electron has absorbed energy and moved up to a higher energy level.
All of its electrons are in the lowest energy levels available to them.
It has absorbed enough energy to lose an electron and become a positive ion.
Its electrons have absorbed energy and now sit between two energy levels.
h: Excitation is the step that comes before an atom gives off light.
w: In the excited state, an electron has absorbed energy and jumped to a higher level. It soon drops back to the ground state and gives off the energy difference as a photon.
x: Electrons all in the lowest available levels is the ground state.
Losing an electron entirely is ionization. An excited electron is still part of the atom.
Electrons can only be in a level, never between levels, because energy is quantized.

q: Which statement about the Bohr model is true?
c: It explains hydrogen’s line spectrum but fails for atoms with more than one electron.
It describes electrons as clouds called orbitals.
It says electrons can have any amount of energy.
It was replaced because it could not explain the line spectrum of hydrogen, the simplest atom.
h: What did Bohr set out to explain, and what happened when the model was tried on other atoms?
w: The Bohr model's quantized energy levels explain hydrogen's lines, and that central idea is still correct. But it fails for atoms with more than one electron, and electrons do not move in neat orbits; the quantum-mechanical model, with orbitals, replaced it.
x: Orbitals belong to the later quantum-mechanical model; Bohr pictured electrons moving in fixed circular orbits.
The central idea of the Bohr model is the opposite: electron energies are quantized.
Hydrogen's spectrum is exactly what the Bohr model gets right; it falls short for other atoms.

q: How many orbitals are in a p subshell, and how many electrons can the subshell hold?
h: Each orbital holds 2 electrons. How many directions do the p orbitals point in?
w: The p subshell has 3 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons, so it holds 6 electrons. That is also why the p block of the periodic table is 6 columns wide.
x: A p subshell is three separate orbitals; a single orbital can never hold more than 2 electrons.
Each of the three orbitals can hold 2 electrons, not 1, so the subshell holds 6.
6 is the number of electrons, not the number of orbitals.

q: How many electrons can the fourth shell (n = 4) hold in all?
h: List the subshells in shell 4 (shell n has n kinds of subshells), then add their capacities.
w: Shell 4 has four subshells: 4s (2), 4p (6), 4d (10) and 4f (14). Total = 32 electrons (2n2 with n = 4).
x: 8 counts only the 4s and 4p subshells; shell 4 also has 4d and 4f.
18 is the capacity of shell 3 (3s, 3p, 3d); shell 4 adds an f subshell.
16 is n2 = 42, the number of orbitals in shell 4; each orbital holds 2 electrons.

q: Which description matches the shapes of s and p orbitals?
c: An s orbital is a sphere; a p orbital has two lobes on opposite sides.
An s orbital has two lobes on opposite sides; a p orbital is a sphere.
Both are spheres around the nucleus, but p orbitals are larger.
Both are flat circles, like the electron orbits in the Bohr model.
h: One of these orbital types has no direction to it; the other points along an axis.
w: An s orbital is a sphere centered on the nucleus (a 2s sphere is bigger than a 1s). A p orbital has two lobes, like a dumbbell, and the three p orbitals point along three perpendicular directions.
x: This swaps the two shapes. Only one of these orbital types points along an axis.
Only one of these orbital types is a sphere. The other one points along an axis.
Orbitals are three-dimensional regions where an electron is likely to be found, not flat circular paths.

q: Following the Aufbau principle, which subshell fills right after 3p?
h: Use the diagonal method; the order is not simply shell by shell.
w: Filling order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s. That is why potassium and calcium, in row 4, put their last electrons in 4s before any 3d electrons appear.
x: 3d comes after 4s; this is the most common filling-order mistake.
4p comes after both 4s and 3d.
There is no 3f subshell: shell 3 has only 3s, 3p and 3d.

q: A student drew this orbital diagram for a ground-state carbon atom. Which rule does it break?
c: It breaks no rule; it is the ground state of carbon.
h: Check whether every lower-energy subshell is full before the next one gets electrons.
w: The diagram shows 2s with one electron and 2p with three. In the ground state, 2s fills before 2p (Aufbau principle). Carbon's ground state is 1s2 2s2 2p2; the drawing is an excited state.
x: The three 2p electrons are spread one per box with the same spin, which is exactly what Hund's rule asks.
No box holds two electrons with the same spin, and none holds more than two.
The diagram has the right count (6), but carbon's ground state is 1s [↑↓] 2s [↑↓] 2p [↑][↑][  ]; moving an electron up from 2s needs energy.

q: Iodide in iodized salt helps the thyroid gland make its hormones. What is the noble-gas configuration of an iodine atom (Z = 53)?
h: Read across row 5 from the start until you reach iodine; remember how the d block is numbered.
w: I is in row 5, group 17. After [Kr] (36 electrons), read across row 5: 5s2, 4d10, 5p5. [Kr] 5s2 4d10 5p5. Check: 36 + 2 + 10 + 5 = 53, and like every halogen it ends in s2 p5.
x: The d block in row 5 is 4d, not 5d: the d shell number is the row number minus 1.
This skips the d block. In row 5 you pass through all ten 4d columns before reaching the p block; the total here is only 43.
Xenon is at the end of iodine's own row; the bracket uses the noble gas from the row above (krypton). This would total 71 electrons.

q: Arsenic, a contaminant in some Central Valley well water, is in row 4, group 15. Which subshell does arsenic's last electron enter?
h: Which block is group 15 in, and how is the shell number of that block related to the row?
w: Arsenic sits in the p block (groups 13 to 18) of row 4, so its last electron enters 4p: As is [Ar] 4s2 3d10 4p3.
x: 3p is the p subshell of row 3 (phosphorus, the element above arsenic, ends in 3p<sup>3</sup>).
3d is the row-4 d block, groups 3 to 12; arsenic has already passed through it.
4d is the d block of row 5, not row 4.

q: What is the electron configuration of the potassium ion, K+?
h: A 1+ charge means one electron was lost. Which shell gives it up first?
w: K is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1. Removing the 4s electron gives 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 (18 electrons), isoelectronic with argon.
x: This adds an electron (20 in all). A positive ion has lost electrons.
Cations lose electrons from the highest-numbered shell first, which is 4s, not 3p.
This is the neutral potassium atom with 19 electrons; the ion has one fewer.

q: A student writes 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> 4p<sup>3</sup> for selenium (Z = 34). What is wrong?
c: The superscripts add to 33 (arsenic); selenium ends in 4p<sup>4</sup>.
The d block in row 4 should be written as 4d.
Nothing is wrong; it is the correct configuration of selenium.
h: Add the superscripts and compare with the atomic number.
w: Total: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 10 + 3 = 33, one short. Selenium is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p4 (34 electrons); the student's version belongs to arsenic.
x: 4s fills before 3d in the diagonal order, so the order written is right.
The row-4 d block is 3d (row number minus 1), so 3d is right.
Add the superscripts and compare with Z = 34.

q: Aluminum is in group 13. Use the octet rule to predict the ion it forms.
h: How many valence electrons does aluminum have, and is it easier to lose those or to gain enough to reach 8?
w: Group 13: 13 − 10 = 3 valence electrons. Aluminum is a metal and loses all 3, forming Al3+ with neon's configuration (10 electrons).
x: Gaining 5 electrons would reach an octet in principle, but a metal with only 3 valence electrons loses them instead.
A 3− charge would mean gaining 3 electrons, which gives 6 valence electrons, not an octet; it also has the sign backward.
Losing just 1 electron would leave 2 valence electrons, not a noble-gas configuration.

q: Why does oxygen form O<sup>2−</sup> rather than O<sup>6+</sup>?
c: Gaining 2 electrons to reach an octet is far easier than losing all 6.
Oxygen has 2 valence electrons, and it gains 2 more.
Oxygen always loses electrons to reach an octet, because it is a nonmetal.
O<sup>2−</sup> has the same number of protons as neon.
h: Count how many steps oxygen is from the nearest noble gas, going each way.
w: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. Gaining 2 reaches an octet (neon's configuration) in 2 steps; losing 6 would take 6. So oxygen forms O2−, oxide.
x: Oxygen is in group 16 and has 6 valence electrons (2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>4</sup>), not 2.
Nonmetals in groups 15 to 17 tend to gain electrons; metals lose them.
O2− has the same number of electrons as neon (10), but it keeps oxygen's 8 protons.

q: Why are the noble gases, such as neon and argon, so unreactive?
c: Their valence shells are already full (an octet, or 2 for helium).
They have no valence electrons at all.
Their atoms are too large to react.
They have only one valence electron, which they hold very tightly.
h: Look at the valence configuration of group 18.
w: Group 18 atoms already have a full valence shell: ns2 np6, an octet (helium: 1s2). They have no electrons to lose easily and no room to gain more, so they barely react.
x: Neon and argon each have 8 valence electrons; the shell is full, not empty.
Noble gases are among the smallest atoms in their rows.
Noble gases have 8 valence electrons (helium has 2), not 1.

q: IV fluid labels give ion amounts in milliequivalents (mEq), a unit that accounts for charge. For which ion does 1 mmol equal 2 mEq?
h: Which of these elements gives up two valence electrons when it forms its ion?
w: Milliequivalents = millimoles × size of the charge. Group 2 calcium loses 2 valence electrons to form Ca2+, so 1 mmol = 2 mEq. Na+, K+ and Cl− each have a charge of size 1. (Context only; this is not dosing guidance.)
x: K<sup>+</sup> has a 1+ charge (group 1), so 1 mmol is 1 mEq.
Na<sup>+</sup> has a 1+ charge (group 1), so 1 mmol is 1 mEq.
Cl<sup>−</sup> has a charge of size 1 (group 17 gains one electron), so 1 mmol is 1 mEq.

q: Na<sup>+</sup> has the same electron configuration as a neon atom. Which statement is true?
c: Na<sup>+</sup> is still sodium, because it has 11 protons.
Na<sup>+</sup> has turned into a neon atom, since it has 10 electrons.
Na<sup>+</sup> has 11 electrons, the same as a sodium atom.
Na<sup>+</sup> has 10 protons, the same number as neon.
h: What decides which element an atom or ion is?
w: Na+ has 11 protons and 10 electrons. It is isoelectronic with neon (10 electrons) but still sodium, because the proton count did not change.
x: Matching neon's electron count does not make it neon. The element is set by the number of protons.
Forming Na⁺ removes one of sodium's 11 electrons, leaving 10.
Forming an ion changes the number of electrons, never the number of protons.

q: Rank Al, P and Cl in order of increasing atomic radius.
h: All three are in the same row. Which way do atoms shrink across a row?
w: Across a period, the nuclear charge grows while electrons go into the same shell, so atomic radius decreases left to right. Increasing radius: Cl < P < Al.
x: This is the order of decreasing radius. Across a row, atoms get smaller, not larger.
Cl is to the right of P, so Cl is smaller than P.
Al is the farthest left of the three, so it is the largest, not in the middle.

q: Which halogen has the lowest first ionization energy?
h: How does ionization energy change going down a group?
w: Going down a group, valence electrons are in higher shells, farther out and more shielded, so ionization energy decreases: F > Cl > Br > I. Iodine is lowest.
x: Fluorine, at the top, holds its electrons the most tightly: it has the highest ionization energy of the group.
Chlorine is below fluorine but above bromine and iodine; its electrons are held more tightly than theirs.
Bromine is above iodine, so its valence electrons are held a little more tightly.

q: Which is larger, a chlorine atom (Cl) or a chloride ion (Cl<sup>−</sup>), and why?
c: Cl<sup>−</sup>, because its extra electron adds repulsion and the cloud spreads out.
Cl, because the ion has gained a proton that pulls the electrons in.
Cl, because the added electron is pulled in tighter by the nucleus.
They are the same size, because both have the same 17 protons.
h: Is Cl<sup>−</sup> a cation or an anion? How do those compare with their atoms?
w: Anions are larger than their atoms. Cl− has 18 electrons and 17 protons; the extra electron increases repulsion and the electron cloud spreads out.
x: Ions form by gaining or losing electrons, never protons.
The extra electron adds repulsion without adding any nuclear pull, so the cloud grows, not shrinks.
The proton count is the same, but the number of electrons is not, and that changes the size.

q: Na<sup>+</sup> and K<sup>+</sup> both carry a 1+ charge, but potassium channels in nerve cells sort them by size. Which ion is larger?
c: K<sup>+</sup>, because its outer electrons are in shell 3, not shell 2.
Na<sup>+</sup>, because sodium comes before potassium in the group.
They are the same size, because they have the same 1+ charge.
Na<sup>+</sup>, because it has fewer protons pulling on its electrons.
h: Write the noble-gas configuration of each ion and compare the highest occupied shells.
w: Down a group, ions get larger just as atoms do. K+ (18 electrons, outer shell 3) is larger than Na+ (10 electrons, outer shell 2). Channel proteins use this size difference to pass K+ selectively.
x: Being higher in a group means fewer occupied shells, and fewer shells do not make an ion larger.
Charge alone does not set size. The number of occupied shells matters most here.
Fewer protons, yes, but also one fewer shell. Going down a group, the added shell matters more.

q: Why do atoms get smaller from left to right across a period, even though each one has more electrons?
c: Each step adds a proton but no new shell, so the stronger pull draws electrons closer.
Each step adds a new shell, which squeezes the electrons closer together.
With more electrons, they repel each other less and pack in more tightly.
Atoms on the right lose electrons more easily, which makes them shrink.
h: What is added to the nucleus at each step, and which shell do the new electrons enter?
w: Across a period, every element adds one proton, while its electrons stay in the same shell. Same-shell electrons shield each other poorly, so the effective nuclear charge increases and pulls the valence electrons in.
x: New shells are added going down a group, which makes atoms larger, not smaller.
More electrons mean more repulsion between them, not less.
Atoms on the right have higher ionization energies, so they hold their electrons more tightly.

q: Ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4, is a nitrogen fertilizer used on many Valley farms. How many atoms in total are in one formula unit?
h: Multiply only what is inside the parentheses by the subscript after them; then add everything up.
w: N: 2; H: 4 × 2 = 8; S: 1; O: 4. Total = 15 atoms. The sulfate group is outside the parentheses, so it is counted once.
x: This counts the ammonium group only once (1 N + 4 H + 1 S + 4 O). The subscript 2 after the parentheses doubles the N and the H.
This doubles the sulfate as well. The 2 belongs to the parentheses around NH<sub>4</sub>; the S and O come after it and are not multiplied.
This is the number of different elements (N, H, S and O), not the number of atoms.

q: Tooth enamel is mostly hydroxyapatite, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2. How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit?
h: Oxygen appears in two different sets of parentheses. Count each set separately.
w: Phosphate: 6 × 4 = 24 O. Hydroxide: 2 × 1 = 2 O. Total = 26 O atoms (along with 10 Ca, 6 P and 2 H).
x: This counts the oxygen in the phosphate groups but leaves out the oxygen in the two hydroxide groups.
This counts the hydroxide oxygen only once. The subscript 2 after (OH) means two hydroxide groups, so two O atoms.
This adds the oxygen subscripts inside the parentheses (4 + 1) without multiplying by the subscripts outside them.

q: Which compound is ionic even though every element in it is a nonmetal?
h: One cation in this course contains no metal at all.
w: A formula that starts with a metal or with NH4 is ionic. NH4Cl contains ammonium ions and chloride ions, so it is ionic even though N, H and Cl are all nonmetals.
x: N and Cl are both nonmetals and the formula has no ammonium ion, so this is a molecular compound (nitrogen trichloride).
This formula starts with H and is dissolved in water, so it is an acid (hydrochloric acid).
C and Cl are both nonmetals sharing electrons, so this is a molecular compound (carbon tetrachloride).

q: Which of these compounds is molecular?
h: Find the staircase line on the periodic table. Which first element is to its right?
w: Molecular compounds contain only nonmetals. Na, Zn and Al are metals, so their oxides are ionic; N2O contains only nitrogen and oxygen, so it is molecular.
x: Na is a metal (group 1), so Na<sub>2</sub>O is made of Na<sup>+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup> ions: ionic.
Zn is a metal, so ZnO is made of Zn<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup> ions: ionic.
Al is a metal, so Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is made of Al<sup>3+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup> ions: ionic.

q: What is the formula of the ionic compound formed by calcium and nitrogen?
h: Write each ion with its charge first. Calcium is in group 2; nitrogen is in group 15.
w: Ca2+ and N3−. Swap-drop gives Ca3N2; 3 × 2 = 6 and 2 × 3 = 6, so the charges cancel and no reducing is needed.
x: This gives each ion its own charge as its subscript. In swap-drop, each charge number goes to the other ion. Check: 2(2+) + 3(3−) is not zero.
This ignores the charges. One Ca<sup>2+</sup> and one N<sup>3−</sup> leave a 1− charge, so the compound would not be neutral.
The subscripts are right, but the cation always comes first in an ionic formula.

q: What is the formula of ammonium sulfide?
h: Treat ammonium as one unit, and check the ending of the anion name.
w: NH4+ and S2−. Swap-drop gives 2 ammonium and 1 sulfide: (NH4)2S. Check: 2(1+) + (2−) = 0.
x: Without parentheses, the 2 runs into the 4 and reads as "42 hydrogen atoms." Put ammonium in parentheses.
One NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> and one S<sup>2−</sup> leave a 1− charge.
This is ammonium sulfate. Sulfide (-ide) is S<sup>2−</sup> alone; sulfate (-ate) is SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>.

q: Chromium(III) ions combine with hydroxide ions. What is the formula of the compound?
h: The Roman numeral tells you the charge of the chromium ion.
w: Cr3+ and OH−. Swap-drop gives 1 Cr and 3 OH: Cr(OH)3. Check: (3+) + 3(1−) = 0.
x: Without parentheses, the 3 applies only to H, so this would mean one O and three H atoms. The 3 should count whole OH groups.
This puts the 3 on chromium. Three Cr<sup>3+</sup> and one OH<sup>−</sup> give 9+ + 1−, not zero.
Two hydroxides would balance a 2+ ion. The Roman numeral III says this chromium ion is 3+.

q: What is the charge on each cobalt ion in Co2O3?
h: Find the total negative charge from the oxide ions, then share it among the metal ions.
w: Total negative charge: 3 × (2−) = 6−. The two Co ions must carry 6+ together, so each is Co3+. Check: 2(3+) + 3(2−) = 0.
x: This reads the subscript 2 as the charge. Subscripts count ions; the charge has to be worked out from the anions.
6+ is the total positive charge of both cobalt ions together. Divide by the 2 cobalt ions.
The cobalt ion is the cation in this compound, so its charge is positive.

q: What is the charge on each iron ion in Fe3(PO4)2?
h: Phosphate is 3−. How much negative charge do two of them carry?
w: Total negative charge: 2 × (3−) = 6−. Three Fe ions carry 6+ together, so each is Fe2+. Check: 3(2+) + 2(3−) = 0.
x: This reads the subscript 3 as the charge. The 3 counts iron ions; work out the charge from the phosphates.
6+ is the total for all three iron ions. Divide by 3.
3− is the charge of the phosphate ion, the anion. Iron is the cation, so its charge is positive.

q: Calcium oxalate, CaC<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, is the most common compound in kidney stones. The calcium ion is Ca<sup>2+</sup>. What is the charge of the oxalate ion?
h: The total charge of the formula unit is zero, and there is one of each ion.
w: Ca2+ + oxalate = 0, so oxalate is 2−: C2O42−, as on the polyatomic ion list.
x: This reads the subscript 4 on O as the charge. Subscripts inside a polyatomic ion count its atoms, not its charge.
One Ca<sup>2+</sup> with a 1− ion would leave a 1+ charge; the formula would need two oxalates.
Oxalate is the anion here, so its charge is negative.

q: In an infant's body, nitrate from well water can be converted to the nitrite ion. What is the formula of the nitrite ion?
h: Start from nitrate. What does -ite change, and what does it leave alone?
w: Nitrate is NO3−; -ite means one fewer O with the same charge, so nitrite is NO2−.
x: This is nitrate, the -ate ion. Nitrite has one fewer oxygen atom.
Removing an O atom does not change the charge. Nitrate and nitrite are both 1−.
This is nitride, the -ide ion: a single N atom with no oxygen.

q: What is the name of the ion ClO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>?
h: Start from chlorate, ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, and count oxygen atoms.
w: Chlorine oxyanions: ClO4− perchlorate, ClO3− chlorate, ClO2− chlorite, ClO− hypochlorite. The charge tells you it is an ion, not the molecule ClO2.
x: Chlorine dioxide is the neutral molecule ClO2. The charge on ClO2− makes it a polyatomic ion with its own name.
Chlorate has three O atoms (ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>); this ion has two.
The hypo- ion has only one O atom (ClO<sup>−</sup>, the ion in bleach).

q: Iodate is IO3−. What is the formula of the periodate ion?
h: Iodine's oxyanions follow the same pattern as chlorine's. What does per- do?
w: Per-...-ate = one more O than -ate, same charge. Iodate is IO3−, so periodate is IO4−.
x: This is iodate itself. The prefix per- adds one O atom.
This has one fewer O than iodate, which is the -ite ion (iodite).
This is iodide, the -ide ion, with no oxygen.

q: What is the formula of the hydrogen phosphate ion?
h: Start from phosphate, PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>. What does adding H<sup>+</sup> do to the charge?
w: PO43− + H+ gives HPO42−, hydrogen phosphate. Each added H+ lowers the negative charge by one.
x: Adding H<sup>+</sup> changes the charge. Each H<sup>+</sup> cancels one negative charge, so 3− becomes 2−.
This has two H atoms: it is dihydrogen phosphate.
Adding a positive H<sup>+</sup> makes the ion less negative, not more.

q: Which pair of ions has the same charge?
h: Which change keeps the charge the same: changing the number of O atoms, or adding H<sup>+</sup>?
w: Changing -ate to -ite (one fewer O) never changes the charge, so nitrate (NO3−) and nitrite (NO2−) are both 1−. Adding H+ or switching to an -ide ion does change it.
x: Nitride is the monatomic N<sup>3−</sup> ion; nitrate is 1−.
Sulfate is 2− and phosphate is 3−.
Carbonate is 2−; adding H<sup>+</sup> makes hydrogen carbonate 1−.

q: What is the name of K<sub>2</sub>S?
h: Is potassium on the fixed-charge list? Is the anion one atom or a polyatomic ion?
w: Cation name + anion name: potassium sulfide. Group 1 metals never get Roman numerals, and ionic names never use prefixes.
x: Ionic names never use prefixes. The charges already fix the ratio of K<sup>+</sup> to S<sup>2−</sup>.
Potassium always forms K<sup>+</sup>, so its name never needs a Roman numeral.
Sulfate is SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>. A single S atom is the -ide ion.

q: What is the name of Co(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?
h: Nitrate is 1−. How many nitrates are there?
w: 2 NO3− = 2−, so cobalt is Co2+: cobalt(II) nitrate (older name cobaltous nitrate).
x: Cobalt forms both Co<sup>2+</sup> and Co<sup>3+</sup>, so the name needs a Roman numeral.
NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is nitrate. Nitrite has only two O atoms (NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>).
The 3 in NO<sub>3</sub> counts oxygen atoms inside the nitrate ion; it is not cobalt's charge. Two 1− nitrates make 2−.

q: Ferrous sulfate is a common iron supplement. What is its formula?
h: Does -ous mean the lower or the higher charge of iron?
w: Ferrous = iron(II) = Fe2+. Fe2+ and SO42− give FeSO4. (Context only; not dosing information.)
x: This is ferric sulfate, iron(III). -ous is the lower charge; -ic is the higher.
Two Fe<sup>2+</sup> and one SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> give 4+ + 2−, not zero.
This is iron(II) sulfide. Sulfate is the polyatomic ion SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>.

q: What is the formula of mercurous nitrate?
h: Mercury(I) is unusual. How is the mercury(I) ion written?
w: Mercurous = mercury(I) = Hg22+. With NO3−: Hg2(NO3)2. Each Hg is 1+, but the ion is the pair.
x: There is no single Hg<sup>+</sup> ion. Mercury(I) is always the pair Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>.
This is mercuric nitrate, mercury(II). -ous is the lower charge.
Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup> has a 2+ charge, so it needs two nitrates, not one.

q: Humidity-indicator cards turn pink when they absorb water to form CoCl<sub>2</sub>·6H<sub>2</sub>O. What is its name?
h: Name the ionic part first, then add a Greek prefix to the word hydrate.
w: 2 Cl− = 2−, so Co2+: cobalt(II) chloride. Six H2O = hexahydrate: cobalt(II) chloride hexahydrate.
x: Cobalt has two possible charges, so the ionic part still needs its Roman numeral.
The prefix goes only on "hydrate." The ionic part is named without prefixes.
Penta- means 5. There are six water molecules here.

q: What is the name of S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>?
h: Two nonmetals: count each kind of atom and use a prefix for each.
w: Molecular: prefix + first element, prefix + second element with -ide. 2 S, 2 Cl: disulfur dichloride.
x: S and Cl are nonmetals, so the name must count the atoms with prefixes.
The second element needs the -ide ending: chloride, not chlorine.
Sulfur dichloride is SCl<sub>2</sub>, with one S. This molecule has two S atoms.

q: In neonatal intensive care, respiratory therapists can deliver inhaled NO to some newborns. What is the systematic name of NO?
h: Mono- appears in one place in this name, but not the other.
w: Nitrogen monoxide: no mono- on the first element; mono- + oxide (with the o dropped) on the second. Its common name is nitric oxide.
x: Mono- is never used on the first element.
Without prefixes, the name does not say which nitrogen oxide this is; N and O form several.
Nitrous oxide is the common name of N<sub>2</sub>O, the dental gas, a different molecule.

q: A student names CaF<sub>2</sub> "calcium difluoride" and SF<sub>2</sub> "sulfur fluoride." Which pair of corrected names is right?
h: Classify each compound first: metal in front, or nonmetals only?
w: Ionic CaF2: calcium fluoride (no prefix). Molecular SF2: sulfur difluoride (prefix required). Same F count, different rules.
x: Calcium is a metal, so CaF<sub>2</sub> is ionic, and ionic names never use prefixes.
SF<sub>2</sub> has two nonmetals and no ion charges, so its name needs a prefix to count the F atoms.
Calcium has a fixed charge, so it never takes a Roman numeral.

q: Why do names of molecular compounds use Greek prefixes, when names of ionic compounds do not?
c: Nonmetals can combine in several ratios with no ion charges to fix them, so the name counts atoms.
Molecular compounds are made of ions with larger charges, so the prefixes give the charges.
Prefixes are used whenever a compound contains oxygen.
Molecular compounds always contain exactly two atoms, so the prefixes are only for spelling.
h: Think of CO and CO<sub>2</sub>. What would happen if both were called "carbon oxide"?
w: Ionic ratios are fixed by charges, so the name does not need to count ions. Molecular compounds have no charges, and the same two nonmetals can form several molecules (CO, CO2), so prefixes count the atoms.
x: Molecular compounds are not made of ions; their atoms share electrons.
Ionic oxides such as Na<sub>2</sub>O are named without prefixes; the rule depends on the compound type, not on oxygen.
Molecules can contain many atoms (for example SF<sub>6</sub>), and the prefixes count them.

q: The common name ammonia refers to which formula?
h: One of these is an ion. Ammonia is a neutral molecule.
w: Ammonia is the neutral molecule NH3: N has 5 valence electrons and makes 3 bonds to H. When NH3 picks up an H+, it becomes the ammonium ion, NH4+.
x: This is the ammonium ion. Ammonia and ammonium sound alike but are different species.
NH<sub>4</sub> without a charge is not a stable molecule; with a 1+ charge it is the ammonium ion.
Ammonia has three hydrogen atoms, not two.

q: What is the name of HI(aq)?
h: Does the formula contain oxygen? Which anion is hiding after the H?
w: The anion is iodide, I−, an -ide ion, so the acid is hydro- + iod + -ic: hydroiodic acid.
x: With no hydro- prefix, this name belongs to an oxyacid made from iodate (IO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>). HI contains no oxygen.
Hydrogen iodide is the name of pure HI, a gas. The (aq) shows it is dissolved in water, so it gets an acid name.
Binary acids always end in -ic. The -ous ending comes from -ite anions.

q: What is the name of H<sub>2</sub>S(aq)?
h: No oxygen means a binary acid. What prefix and ending do binary acids get?
w: Sulfide (-ide) becomes hydro-...-ic: hydrosulfuric acid. Sulfuric acid, H2SO4, is a different compound.
x: Sulfuric acid is H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, an oxyacid from sulfate. H<sub>2</sub>S has no oxygen.
Sulfurous acid is H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>, from sulfite. H<sub>2</sub>S has no oxygen.
Binary acids end in -ic, not -ous.

q: What is the name of HBrO<sub>2</sub>?
h: Name the anion first. How does BrO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> compare with bromate?
w: Name the anion first: BrO2− has one fewer O than bromate (BrO3−), so it is bromite. An -ite anion gives an -ous acid: bromous acid.
x: Bromic acid comes from bromate, BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, with three O atoms.
Oxyacids never take hydro-; that prefix is only for acids without oxygen.
The hypo- acid, HBrO, comes from hypobromite, with only one O.

q: Many colas contain phosphoric acid. What is its formula?
h: The number of H atoms equals the size of the anion's charge.
w: Phosphoric acid comes from the phosphate ion, PO43− (-ate → -ic). It takes 3 H+ to cancel the 3− charge: H3PO4.
x: One H<sup>+</sup> cancels only one of phosphate's three negative charges.
This is phosphorous acid, from phosphite (PO<sub>3</sub><sup>3−</sup>). -ic means the -ate ion.
Two H<sup>+</sup> leave a 1− charge; the acid must be neutral.

q: In water, bleach forms hypochlorous acid, which kills bacteria. What is its formula?
h: Find the anion: hypo-...-ite. How many O atoms does it have?
w: Hypochlorous ← hypochlorite, ClO−; one H+: HClO. Prefixes such as hypo- and per- stay in acid names.
x: This is chlorous acid, from chlorite. The hypo- prefix means one fewer O than chlorite.
This is hydrochloric acid, which has no oxygen.
This is perchloric acid, from perchlorate, with four O atoms.

q: Carbon dioxide dissolved in blood forms H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>. What is its name?
h: Which anion is left when both H<sup>+</sup> are removed?
w: CO32− = carbonate; -ate → -ic: carbonic acid. It releases H+ and bicarbonate in blood.
x: Hydro- is only for acids with no oxygen.
-ous comes from an -ite anion; carbonate is an -ate ion.
Bicarbonate is the HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ion, with one H and a 1− charge.

q: You have 1.00 mol of copper atoms and 1.00 mol of sucrose molecules. Which statement is true?
c: They contain the same number of particles, but the sucrose has more mass.
They have the same mass, because both are 1.00 mol.
The copper contains more particles, because copper atoms are smaller.
The sucrose contains more particles, because each molecule is bigger.
h: A dozen eggs and a dozen bowling balls: same count or same mass?
w: Both samples contain the same number of particles (6.0221 × 1023). 1.00 mol of sucrose has a mass of 342.297 g; 1.00 mol of copper, 63.55 g.
x: Equal moles mean equal numbers of particles, not equal masses. Heavier particles make a heavier mole.
The size of the particle does not change the count. 1.00 mol is always 6.0221 × 10<sup>23</sup> particles.
Bigger particles make a mole heavier, not larger in number.

q: Sodium chloride, NaCl, is an ionic compound. When you count out 1 mol of NaCl, what particles are you counting?
h: What do we call the smallest repeating unit of an ionic compound?
w: 1 mol NaCl = 6.0221 × 1023 formula units, each made of one Na+ ion and one Cl− ion.
x: Ionic compounds have no molecules; molecules are for compounds of nonmetals joined by covalent bonds.
Chlorine in NaCl is present as chloride ions, not as Cl<sub>2</sub> molecules.
Avogadro's number counts particles, not grams. One mole of NaCl has a mass of 58.44 g.

q: Which sample contains the greatest number of atoms?
h: All four samples have the same number of particles. Which particle is made of the most atoms?
w: Same number of molecules (1.0 mol each), so count atoms per particle: CH4 5, H2O 3, O2 2, He 1. 1.0 mol of CH4 has the most atoms, 5.0 mol.
x: Each H<sub>2</sub>O molecule has 3 atoms, so this is 3.0 mol of atoms. Another sample has more atoms per molecule.
Each O<sub>2</sub> molecule has 2 atoms, so this is 2.0 mol of atoms.
Helium exists as single atoms, so this is only 1.0 mol of atoms.

q: A student calculates that 0.50 mol of water contains 8.3 × 10<sup>−25</sup> molecules. What went wrong?
c: The student divided by Avogadro's number instead of multiplying.
The student used the molar mass of water instead of Avogadro's number.
The student should have counted atoms, which would be 3 times larger.
Nothing; half a mole is a very small amount, so the number should be tiny.
h: Use the sanity check: should a particle count be a huge number or a tiny one?
w: 8.3 × 10−25 is less than one molecule, which is impossible. It is 0.50 ÷ NA: the student divided instead of multiplying. The correct count is 3.0 × 1023 molecules.
x: 0.50 mol × 18.015 g/mol = 9.0 g, not 10<sup>−25</sup>. That is not where this number comes from.
Counting atoms would change the number by a factor of 3, not by a factor of about 10<sup>48</sup>.
Half a mole is a small amount of water (about 9 g), but it still holds an enormous number of molecules. No sample can hold less than one molecule.

q: Which sample contains the greatest number of particles?
h: Put every sample in the same unit, either moles or particles, before comparing.
w: In moles: CO2 0.80; H2O 3.0 × 1023 ÷ NA = 0.50; Fe 0.25; NaCl 4.2 × 1023 ÷ NA = 0.70. 0.80 mol of CO2 has the most particles.
x: 3.0 × 10<sup>23</sup> molecules is about 0.50 mol, less than 0.80 mol.
0.25 mol is 1.5 × 10<sup>23</sup> atoms, the smallest count here.
4.2 × 10<sup>23</sup> formula units is about 0.70 mol, a little less than 0.80 mol.

q: Why is the molar mass of an element, in g/mol, the same number as its atomic mass in amu?
c: Avogadro’s number was chosen to make the gram mass of a mole equal the atomic mass in amu.
One gram is defined as one amu.
Every atom has a mass of exactly 1 amu, so molar mass and atomic mass always match.
It is a coincidence that holds only for carbon-12, the isotope the amu scale is based on.
h: How was the size of a mole chosen?
w: NA was chosen so that the mass of 1 mol in grams equals the mass of one particle in amu. So one carbon atom averages 12.011 amu and one mole of carbon has a mass of 12.011 g.
x: One amu is about 1.66 × 10<sup>−24</sup> g, far smaller than a gram. It takes Avogadro's number of amu to make 1 g.
Atoms have different masses (H 1.008 amu, Fe 55.85 amu); that is why molar masses differ.
It holds for every element and compound: Na is 22.99 amu per atom and 22.99 g per mole.

q: Glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, has a molar mass of 180.156 g/mol. Which statement is correct?
c: One molecule is 180.156 amu, and one mole is 180.156 g.
One glucose molecule has a mass of 180.156 g.
One mole of glucose has a mass of 180.156 amu.
One glucose molecule has a mass of 180.156 g/mol.
h: One particle: which unit? One mole: which unit?
w: One molecule: 180.156 amu. One mole: 180.156 g. Molar mass, 180.156 g/mol, links the two.
x: 180.156 g is the mass of 6.0221 × 10<sup>23</sup> molecules. One molecule is far lighter (about 3 × 10<sup>−22</sup> g).
A mole is a huge number of molecules, so its mass is in grams; amu is for one particle.
g/mol is the unit of molar mass, the mass per mole. One molecule's mass is in amu (or grams).

q: Gypsum, calcium sulfate dihydrate (CaSO<sub>4</sub>·2H<sub>2</sub>O), is the raw material for the plaster and dental stone used to pour dental models. What is its molar mass? (Ca 40.08, S 32.06, O 15.999, H 1.008)
h: The dot in a hydrate means “plus.” How many waters are added?
x: This is anhydrous calcium sulfate. The ·2H<sub>2</sub>O adds the mass of two waters.
This treats the dot as “times” and doubles the whole formula. The dot means “plus”: add 2 × 18.015.
This adds only one water. The 2 in front of H<sub>2</sub>O means two water molecules per formula unit.

q: A fasting blood glucose is reported as 126 mg/dL. Glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, has a molar mass of 180.156 g/mol. What is this value in mmol/L?
h: Change dL to L first, then use molar mass as 180.156 mg per mmol.
w: 126 mg/dL × 10 dL/L = 1260 mg/L; 1260 mg/L ÷ 180.156 mg/mmol = 6.99 mmol/L. (Context only; use the units on the facility's meter.)
x: This skips the dL → L step. There are 10 dL in 1 L, so the value per liter is 10 times larger.
This is the value in mol/L, labeled mmol/L. Using mg with mg/mmol gives millimoles directly.
This multiplies by the molar mass; mass to moles means dividing.

q: Nitrous oxide, N2O (44.013 g/mol), is the “laughing gas” used for sedation in some dental offices. What is the mass of one N2O molecule?
h: Mass per molecule = mass of one mole ÷ molecules in one mole.
w: 44.013 g/mol ÷ 6.0221 × 1023 molecules/mol = 7.3086 × 10−23 g per molecule (5 significant figures, since 44.013 and 6.0221 both have 5).
x: This multiplies by Avogadro's number; one molecule must be far lighter than a mole, not heavier.
This divides Avogadro's number by the molar mass, which gives molecules per gram, not grams per molecule.
44.013 g is the mass of a whole mole. One molecule is 44.013 amu.

q: Thyroxine, C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>11</sub>I<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>4</sub> (776.86 g/mol), is the main hormone made by the thyroid gland. A daily thyroid-replacement dose is on the order of 0.150 mg. How many thyroxine molecules are in 0.150 mg?
h: Change mg to g first, then go through moles.
w: 1.50 × 10−4 g × (1 mol / 776.86 g) × (6.0221 × 1023 / 1 mol) = 1.16 × 1017 molecules. Even a tiny tablet dose is an enormous number of molecules.
x: This skips the mg → g step, so the answer is 1000 times too large. The molar mass is in g/mol.
This stops at moles. One more step gives molecules.
This multiplies by the molar mass instead of dividing in the first step.

q: Which sample has the greatest mass? Use the molar masses H2O 18.015, CO2 44.009, NH3 17.031, and C6H12O6 180.156 g/mol.
h: Convert every sample to grams: moles × molar mass (and particles ÷ N<sub>A</sub> first).
w: Masses: C6H12O6 18 g, H2O 9.0 g, CO2 8.8 g, NH3 8.5 g. 0.10 mol of glucose has the greatest mass: the most moles is not always the most grams.
x: 0.50 mol × 18.015 g/mol = 9.0 g. More moles, but each molecule is light.
0.20 mol × 44.009 g/mol = 8.8 g.
3.0 × 10<sup>23</sup> ÷ 6.0221 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 0.50 mol; × 17.031 g/mol = 8.5 g.

q: Calcium chloride, CaCl2, dissolves into Ca2+ and Cl− ions. How many ions in total are released by 0.0450 mol of CaCl2?
h: How many ions come from one formula unit of CaCl<sub>2</sub>?
w: 1 Ca2+ + 2 Cl− = 3 ions per formula unit. 0.0450 mol × 3 = 0.135 mol ions = 8.13 × 1022 ions.
x: This counts only the chloride ions. Add the calcium ions.
This counts formula units, not the ions they release.
This counts the 2+ charge as two ions. Ca<sup>2+</sup> is one ion with a 2+ charge.

q: An iron supplement tablet contains 325 mg of ferrous fumarate, FeC<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (169.91 g/mol). How many milligrams of elemental iron does it provide? (Fe 55.85)
h: mg compound → mmol compound → mmol Fe → mg Fe.
w: 325 mg × (1 mmol / 169.91 mg) × (1 mmol Fe / 1 mmol) × (55.85 mg / 1 mmol Fe) = 107 mg Fe, about a third of the tablet's mass. (Context only; follow the label.)
x: This stops at millimoles of ferrous fumarate (1.91 mmol) and labels it mg. One more step, with the molar mass of Fe, gives the mass of iron.
This uses both molar masses upside down; the iron cannot weigh more than the whole tablet compound.
This uses 26, iron's atomic number, instead of its molar mass, 55.85.

q: A CT contrast dose contains 32.4 g of iohexol, C<sub>19</sub>H<sub>26</sub>I<sub>3</sub>N<sub>3</sub>O<sub>9</sub> (821.13 g/mol). What mass of iodine does it contain? (I 126.90)
h: g iohexol → mol iohexol → mol I (subscript) → g I.
w: 32.4 g × (1 mol / 821.13 g) × (3 mol I / 1 mol) × (126.90 g / 1 mol I) = 15.0 g I, almost half the mass of the drug.
x: This skips the subscript 3; each iohexol molecule carries three iodine atoms.
This uses 53, iodine's atomic number, instead of its molar mass, 126.90.
This divides by 3 instead of multiplying. Each iohexol molecule carries three iodine atoms, so there are three times as many moles of I as moles of iohexol.

q: To find the grams of oxygen in 2.00 mol of CO<sub>2</sub>, which molar mass should you use for oxygen in the last step?
c: 15.999 g/mol, because the formula counts O atoms
44.009 g/mol, the molar mass of the whole CO<sub>2</sub>
h: After the subscript step, what particle do your moles count?
w: 2.00 mol CO2 × 2 = 4.00 mol O atoms; × 15.999 g/mol = 64.0 g O.
x: Oxygen is diatomic only as the free element, O<sub>2</sub>. In CO<sub>2</sub> it is present as atoms.
That converts moles of CO<sub>2</sub> to grams of CO<sub>2</sub>, not grams of oxygen.
8 is the number of protons, not the mass of a mole of atoms.

q: Which pair of elements is most likely to form an ionic bond?
h: Look for a metal paired with a nonmetal.
w: Metal + nonmetal means electron transfer: Mg and O form the ionic compound MgO. (Their electronegativity difference, 3.5 − 1.2 = 2.3, is also above 2.0.)
x: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals; they share electrons (covalent bonds), as in CO<sub>2</sub>.
Nitrogen and hydrogen are both nonmetals; they share electrons, as in NH<sub>3</sub>.
Copper and zinc are both metals. Neither one needs extra electrons, so there is no metal-to-nonmetal transfer.

q: Aluminum and fluorine form an ionic compound. How many fluorine atoms are needed to accept the electrons from one aluminum atom?
h: How many electrons does Al lose? How many can one F accept?
w: Al → Al3+ + 3 e−; each F + 1 e− → F−. Electrons lost (3) = electrons gained (3 × 1), so 3 F atoms: AlF3.
x: One F atom can accept only one electron, leaving Al with two more to give.
Two F atoms take 2 electrons, but Al gives away 3.
7 is the number of valence electrons fluorine already has, not the number of F atoms needed.

q: Which property is typical of an ionic compound such as sodium chloride?
c: A hard, brittle solid with a high melting point
A soft solid that melts below 100 °C
A solid that conducts electricity well
A substance made of separate NaCl molecules
h: Picture the crystal lattice. How many attractions hold each ion in place?
w: Ionic solids are lattices of cations and anions: hard, brittle, high-melting, and conducting only when melted or dissolved.
x: Low melting points are typical of molecular substances such as wax or sugar, not ionic lattices.
In the solid, the ions are locked in place, so solid ionic compounds do not conduct.
Ionic compounds have no molecules. NaCl is a lattice; the formula gives the ratio of ions (a formula unit).

q: Which sample conducts electricity?
c: Calcium chloride melted at high temperature
Solid calcium chloride crystals at room temperature
h: Electric current needs charged particles that can move. Which sample has mobile ions?
w: Only an ionic compound that is melted or dissolved has moving ions. Melted calcium chloride conducts; the solid does not, and sugar (molecular) never forms ions.
x: In the solid, the Ca<sup>2+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions are locked in the lattice and cannot move.
Sugar is a molecular compound; it has no ions to carry a current.
Sugar dissolves as whole, neutral molecules, not ions, so the solution does not conduct.

q: How many valence electrons are in the hydronium ion, H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>?
h: Add the group numbers, then adjust for the charge. Does a 1+ charge add or remove an electron?
w: Add the valence electrons: O has 6 and each H has 1, so 6 + 3(1) = 9. A 1+ charge means one electron was lost: 9 − 1 = 8 valence electrons.
x: This forgets the charge. A positive ion has lost an electron.
This adds an electron for the charge. Add for negative charges, subtract for positive charges.
This counts 8 for O and 2 for each H, the electrons each atom will end up with, not the valence electrons available.

q: Which describes the Lewis structure of nitrogen gas, N<sub>2</sub>, which makes up 78% of air?
c: N≡N, with one lone pair on each N
N=N, with two lone pairs on each N
N–N, with three lone pairs on each N
h: N<sub>2</sub> has 10 valence electrons. Which picture uses exactly 10 and gives each N an octet?
w: 2 × 5 = 10 electrons. A single bond leaves N short, so lone pairs move into bonds until N≡N with one lone pair on each N (6 + 2 + 2 = 10).
x: This uses 4 + 8 = 12 electrons, but N<sub>2</sub> has only 2 × 5 = 10.
This uses 2 + 12 = 14 electrons, more than the 10 available. Never add electrons to complete octets.
This uses only 6 electrons and leaves each N with 6, not 8.

q: Methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, has 14 valence electrons. Which structure is correct?
c: H<sub>3</sub>C–O–H, with two lone pairs on O
H<sub>3</sub>C–H–O, with three lone pairs on O
H<sub>3</sub>C–O–H, with three lone pairs on O
h: The formula is written in groups: a CH<sub>3</sub> group bonded to an OH group. Then count electrons.
w: 4 + 4(1) + 6 = 14 electrons: H3C–O–H with two lone pairs on O. Check: 5 × 2 + 2 × 2 = 14.
x: This puts H in the middle with two bonds. Hydrogen forms only one bond, so it is never central.
This uses only 10 electrons and leaves O with 4. Outer and inner O atoms keep their lone pairs.
This uses 16 electrons, more than the 14 available, and gives O 10 electrons.

q: Phosgene, COCl<sub>2</sub>, has C as the central atom and 24 valence electrons. Which Lewis structure is correct?
c: C single-bonded to each Cl and double-bonded to O; 2 lone pairs on O and 3 on each Cl
C single-bonded to O and to each Cl; 3 lone pairs on O and 3 on each Cl
C double-bonded to O and to one Cl, single-bonded to the other Cl; 2 lone pairs on O, 2 on the double-bonded Cl, 3 on the other Cl
C single-bonded to O and to each Cl; 1 lone pair on C, 3 on O, and 3 on each Cl
h: Start with single bonds and lone pairs. Is C short of an octet? Which atom (O or Cl) usually forms a double bond?
w: Single bonds use 6, lone pairs on O and Cl use 18 (24 total), but C has only 6. One O lone pair moves into a bond: C=O with two C–Cl bonds. O forms 2 bonds (HONC), Cl forms 1.
x: This uses 24 electrons, but C has only 3 bonds (6 electrons). Move a lone pair from O into a C=O double bond.
This gives C 5 bonds (10 electrons), breaking the octet, and gives Cl two bonds. Halogens usually form one bond.
This uses 26 electrons, 2 more than are available. Make a double bond; never add electrons.

q: Which describes the Lewis structure of the ammonium ion, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>?
c: N bonded to four H atoms, no lone pairs, in brackets with a 1+ charge
N bonded to four H atoms, one lone pair on N, in brackets with a 1+ charge
N bonded to three H atoms, one lone pair on N, and the fourth H bonded to another H
N bonded to four H atoms, no lone pairs, in brackets with a 1− charge
h: Count electrons (subtract one for the 1+ charge), then place bonds.
w: NH4+: 5 + 4(1) − 1 = 8 electrons = four N–H bonds and no lone pairs, drawn as [NH4]+.
x: This uses 10 electrons, the count you get by adding (not subtracting) an electron for the 1+ charge, and gives N 10 electrons.
One H would have two bonds. Hydrogen forms only one bond.
The bonds are right, but the charge is wrong. A 1− ion would have 10 electrons; this structure has 8, so it is 1+.

q: Ground-level ozone, O<sub>3</sub>, is the main summer smog pollutant in the San Joaquin Valley. Its central O atom has one double bond, one single bond, and one lone pair. What is the shape of O<sub>3</sub>?
h: Count groups on the central O: each bond is one group, and so is the lone pair.
w: Central O: 1 double + 1 single + 1 lone pair = 3 groups, 1 lone pair: bent, about 120°.
x: Bent at about 109.5° is the 4-group bent shape (2 lone pairs, as in water). The central O in ozone has 3 groups.
Linear needs 2 groups. The lone pair on the central O is a third group.
Trigonal planar is the electron geometry; the shape names only the three O atoms.

q: In acetylene, H–C≡C–H, what is the shape around each carbon atom?
h: How many groups are on each C? A triple bond counts once.
w: Each C: 1 single + 1 triple = 2 groups, no lone pairs: linear, 180°. The whole molecule is a straight line.
x: This counts the triple bond as three groups (1 + 3 = 4). A triple bond is one group.
Three groups would need another bond or a lone pair on C; each C has only two groups.
Each C has no lone pairs, so there is nothing to bend it.

q: Which molecule is trigonal planar?
h: Trigonal planar needs 3 groups and no lone pairs on the central atom.
w: Only CH2O has 3 groups and 0 lone pairs. NH3 and PCl3 are trigonal pyramidal (4 groups, 1 lone pair); O3 is bent.
x: N has 3 bonds plus a lone pair: 4 groups, trigonal pyramidal.
P has 3 bonds plus a lone pair: 4 groups, trigonal pyramidal. Three outer atoms are not enough for trigonal planar.
The central O has 3 groups, but one is a lone pair, so ozone is bent.

q: Why do CH<sub>4</sub> and NH<sub>3</sub> have different shapes, even though both central atoms have four electron groups?
c: Shape names only atom positions; N has a lone pair in place of a fourth atom.
N has fewer electron groups than C.
Lone pairs do not take up any space around the central atom.
C is a larger atom than N, so its four bonds spread out more widely.
h: Compare electron geometry with molecular shape.
w: Both have 4 groups (tetrahedral electron geometry), but the shape names only atoms: CH4 tetrahedral; NH3 (1 lone pair) trigonal pyramidal.
x: Both have 4 groups: C has 4 bonds; N has 3 bonds + 1 lone pair.
Lone pairs take up space (a little more than bonds); that is why they still push the bonds into a pyramid.
Atom size is not what VSEPR uses. The difference is a lone pair versus a bond.

q: The hydronium ion, H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, has three O–H bonds and one lone pair on O. What is its shape?
h: An ion is handled exactly like a molecule: count groups on the central atom.
w: O has 4 electron groups (3 bonds + 1 lone pair), so the electron geometry is tetrahedral. The shape names only the atoms, and with one corner taken by a lone pair the H atoms form a trigonal pyramid, about 109.5° apart, like NH3.
x: This ignores the lone pair. It is a fourth group and pushes the H atoms out of the plane.
Tetrahedral is the electron geometry; one corner is a lone pair, which is not named in the shape.
Bent (4 groups) would need 2 lone pairs and 2 bonds.

q: Which statement describes the periodic trend in electronegativity?
c: It increases across a period and decreases down a group.
It decreases across a period and increases down a group.
It increases across a period and increases down a group.
It is about the same for every element in a group.
h: Where is fluorine on the periodic table?
w: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group; fluorine (4.0) is highest.
x: This reverses both directions. F (upper right) is the most electronegative element.
Down a group, the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus, so the pull on shared electrons decreases (F 4.0, Cl 3.0).
Values change down a group: F 4.0, Cl 3.0, Br 2.8, I 2.5.

q: Nitrogen dioxide from vehicle exhaust helps form the Valley's summer ozone. What is ΔEN for an N–O bond, and what kind of bond is it? (N 3.0, O 3.5)
h: Subtract the smaller value from the larger, then compare with 0.4 and 2.0.
w: ΔEN = 3.5 − 3.0 = 0.5. That is above 0.4 and below 2.0, so the bond is polar covalent, with δ− on the more electronegative O.
x: This adds the values. ΔEN is a difference: subtract the smaller from the larger.
0.5 is just above the 0–0.4 nonpolar range, so the bond is polar covalent.
Subtract the smaller value from the larger, so ΔEN is never negative; 0.5 is in the polar covalent range.

q: In an O–H bond, which atom carries the partial negative charge (δ−), and which way does the dipole arrow point? (O 3.5, H 2.1)
c: O is δ−; the arrow points toward O
H is δ−; the arrow points toward H
O is δ−; the arrow points toward H
Neither; the O–H bond is nonpolar
h: The more electronegative atom gets the electrons, the δ−, and the arrowhead.
w: O–H: ΔEN = 1.4, polar covalent. O is δ−, and the dipole arrow points toward O (cross at H).
x: H is the less electronegative atom, so it is the δ+ end.
The partial charges are right, but the arrow points toward the δ− atom, not away from it.
ΔEN = 3.5 − 2.1 = 1.4, well above 0.4: the bond is polar.

q: In the lungs, O<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> cross the thin, fatty membranes of the alveoli and capillaries very quickly. Which statement explains this?
c: Both are polar molecules, like water.
CO<sub>2</sub> is polar and O<sub>2</sub> is nonpolar.
Both are ionic compounds that dissolve in the membrane.
h: Decide the polarity of each gas: O=O, and O=C=O (linear).
w: Both are small nonpolar molecules, so they slip through the nonpolar membrane; ions such as Na+ need protein channels.
x: Neither is polar. O<sub>2</sub> has no polar bonds; CO<sub>2</sub>'s bond dipoles cancel.
CO<sub>2</sub> has polar bonds, but its linear shape cancels them, so the molecule is nonpolar.
Both are molecules of nonmetals held by covalent bonds; neither contains ions.

q: Iron tablets often contain ferrous sulfate heptahydrate, FeSO<sub>4</sub>·7H<sub>2</sub>O (278.01 g/mol). What percent of this compound's mass is iron? (Fe 55.85)
h: Use the molar mass of the whole hydrate, water included.
w: %Fe = 55.85 ÷ 278.01 × 100% = 20.09%. A 325 mg tablet of this hydrate holds about 65 mg of iron. (Context only.)
x: This uses the molar mass of anhydrous FeSO<sub>4</sub> (151.91). The tablet compound includes 7 waters.
This adds only one water. The 7 in front of H<sub>2</sub>O means seven waters.
This divides the wrong way; a part cannot be more than 100% of the whole.

q: One sample of pure sodium chloride comes from sea salt, and another is mined rock salt from a different continent. What does the law of constant composition say about them?
c: Both have the same mass percent of sodium.
The larger sample has the higher mass percent of sodium.
Their percents differ, because they come from different places.
Both are 50% sodium, because NaCl has one Na and one Cl.
h: What stays the same for every pure sample of a compound?
w: Law of constant composition (definite proportions): every pure sample of NaCl has the same mass percent of sodium.
x: Percent composition does not depend on sample size; that is the point of a percent.
The source does not matter for a pure compound. (Impurities in unrefined salt would change the measured percent, but not the composition of NaCl itself.)
Equal numbers of atoms do not mean equal masses: Na (22.99) is lighter than Cl (35.45).

q: Heating 1.200 g of copper in air produces 1.502 g of a black copper oxide. What is the mass percent of oxygen in the oxide?
h: By conservation of mass, oxygen = product − metal. Then part ÷ whole.
x: This divides by the copper mass. The whole is the oxide product, 1.502 g.
This is the percent of copper, not oxygen.
This adds the copper and oxide masses. The oxide mass already includes the copper.

q: Butane, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, is lighter fluid. What is its empirical formula?
h: Find the largest number that divides every subscript.
w: Divide every subscript by the largest number that divides them all, here 2: C4H10 ÷ 2 = C2H5. Because 5 is odd, the 2 : 5 ratio cannot be reduced further. CH2 is a trap: it rounds the ratio to 1 : 2, which is not the true ratio of C to H in butane.
x: 4 and 10 share a factor of 2, so this is not the simplest ratio.
This is close to 1 : 2.5 but rounded. Subscripts must be whole numbers in the exact ratio.
This multiplies by 2 instead of dividing. The empirical formula is the smallest ratio.

q: Magnetite, a magnetic iron ore, is 72.36% Fe and 27.64% O by mass. What is its empirical formula? (Fe 55.85, O 15.999)
h: After dividing by the smaller, a value near 1.33 is a signal, not a rounding error.
x: This rounds 1.33 down to 1. A ratio near 1.33 means multiply by 3.
Multiplying 1 : 1.333 by 2 gives 2 : 2.67, still not whole numbers. Use 3.
This inverts the ratio; there are more moles of O than of Fe.

q: Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate hydrate, MgSO<sub>4</sub>·xH<sub>2</sub>O. Heating 3.000 g of it leaves 1.465 g of anhydrous MgSO<sub>4</sub> (120.37 g/mol). What is x? (H<sub>2</sub>O 18.015 g/mol)
h: Water = mass lost. Convert water and salt to moles, then divide.
w: 1.535 g ÷ 18.015 g/mol = 0.08521 mol H2O; 1.465 g ÷ 120.37 g/mol = 0.01217 mol MgSO4; ratio 7.00: x = 7, MgSO4·7H2O.
x: This compares grams of water and salt (1.535 : 1.465), not moles.
This divides by the moles of hydrate as if 3.000 g were anhydrous MgSO<sub>4</sub>; use the 1.465 g that is left after heating.
This treats the whole 3.000 g as water. Only the mass lost on heating is water.

q: Which observation is the best evidence that a chemical reaction has occurred?
c: Two clear, colorless solutions are mixed, and a yellow solid forms.
A pot of water on the stove forms bubbles as it heats.
A spoonful of sugar disappears when it is stirred into a cup of hot tea.
An ice cube melts into a puddle on the counter.
h: Ask: did a new substance form, or did the same substance just change form?
w: A new solid appearing from clear solutions is a precipitate, one of the four signs of reaction (gas, precipitate, color change, energy change).
x: Bubbles in boiling water are water vapor, the same substance in a new state: a physical change.
Dissolving is a physical change; the sugar molecules are still sugar, now spread through the water.
Melting changes only the state of water, not its identity.

q: Each of these fizzes. Which one is a physical change, not a chemical reaction?
c: A bottle of soda is opened, and dissolved carbon dioxide escapes as bubbles.
An antacid tablet containing calcium carbonate is dropped into hydrochloric acid.
Hydrogen peroxide is poured on a cut, where the enzyme catalase breaks it into water and oxygen gas.
Baking soda is stirred into vinegar.
h: Bubbles are a clue, not proof. Was the gas already there, or was it made?
w: Opening a soda only releases gas that was already dissolved; the other three make new substances, including a new gas.
x: Calcium carbonate reacts with the acid to make new substances, including CO<sub>2</sub> gas.
Catalase speeds up the decomposition of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> into new substances, H<sub>2</sub>O and O<sub>2</sub>: a chemical change.
Baking soda and acetic acid react to make sodium acetate, water, and new CO<sub>2</sub> gas.

q: A student heats baking soda, NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, in an open crucible: 2 NaHCO<sub>3</sub>(s) → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>(s) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g). Using the data in the table, what total mass of water vapor and carbon dioxide escaped?
h: The mass lost by the open crucible is the mass of the gases that escaped.
w: Gases escaped = 31.62 g − 28.52 g = 3.10 g. In a sealed container the total mass would not change.
x: This adds the two readings. The gases leaving are the difference between them.
28.52 g is what is left in the crucible, not what escaped.
Mass is conserved overall, but the gases left the open crucible, so the crucible's mass drops.

q: Balance the equation: Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>(aq) + KOH(aq) → Al(OH)<sub>3</sub>(s) + K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq). What are the coefficients, in order?
h: Balance Al first, then the polyatomic units OH and SO<sub>4</sub>, then check K.
w: 1, 6, 2, 3: Al2(SO4)3(aq) + 6 KOH(aq) → 2 Al(OH)3(s) + 3 K2SO4(aq). Al 2 = 2; SO4 3 = 3; K 6 = 6; OH 6 = 6.
x: Everything balances, but all four coefficients share a factor of 2.
Al and sulfate balance, but OH does not: 3 on the left, 6 on the right (and K: 3 vs 6).
Aluminum does not balance: 2 Al on the left, 1 on the right.

q: A student balances H<sub>2</sub>(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g) → HCl(g) by changing it to H<sub>2</sub>(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g) → H<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>(g). What is wrong?
c: Changing a subscript makes a new substance; put a 2 in front of HCl instead.
Nothing is wrong, because the atoms now balance.
The reactants should be written as single atoms, H and Cl, so that HCl balances.
The fix should be a coefficient of 2 in front of H<sub>2</sub> instead.
h: What are you allowed to change when balancing: subscripts or coefficients?
w: Never change subscripts. H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2 HCl(g): H 2 = 2, Cl 2 = 2.
x: Atoms balance, but H<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> is not the product. Balancing must keep the correct formulas.
Hydrogen and chlorine are diatomic elements, H<sub>2</sub> and Cl<sub>2</sub>; writing H or Cl changes the substances.
A 2 in front of H<sub>2</sub> gives 4 H on the left and still only 1 on the right.

q: In a blast furnace, solid iron(III) oxide reacts with carbon monoxide gas to form solid iron and carbon dioxide gas. Which equation is correct, balanced, and labeled?
h: Names first (iron(III) oxide = Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>), then balance Fe, C, and O, then add labels.
w: Fe2O3(s) + 3 CO(g) → 2 Fe(s) + 3 CO2(g). Check: Fe 2 = 2, C 3 = 3, O 6 = 6.
x: Iron balances, but O does not: 4 on the left, 2 on the right.
Carbon dioxide is described as a gas, so its label is (g), not (aq).
Iron(III) oxide is Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (from Fe<sup>3+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup>); the formula cannot be changed.

q: What type of reaction is AgNO<sub>3</sub>(aq) + KBr(aq) → AgBr(s) + KNO<sub>3</sub>(aq)?
h: Two compounds on the left, two on the right, partners exchanged.
w: The cations trade anions: double displacement (a precipitation, since AgBr is insoluble).
x: Single displacement needs a free element as a reactant. Both reactants here are compounds.
Combination makes one product; this makes two.
Decomposition starts with one reactant; this has two.

q: Which reaction is a combination reaction?
h: Look for exactly one product.
w: Only 2 Ca + O2 → 2 CaO makes a single product from two reactants.
x: A carbon fuel reacting with O<sub>2</sub> to give CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O is combustion (a welding torch).
One reactant breaking into two products is decomposition (the reaction that inflates an air bag).
An element replacing a metal ion in a compound is single displacement.

q: Calcium metal heated in nitrogen gas forms calcium nitride. Which equation correctly predicts and balances the product?
h: Predict the formula from charges first (nitride is N<sup>3−</sup>), then balance.
w: Write the product from the ion charges: Ca2+ and N3− need 3 Ca for every 2 N, so it is Ca3N2. Then balance: 3 Ca on the left, and one N2 supplies the 2 N. 3 Ca(s) + N2(g) → Ca3N2(s).
x: This copies the subscript from N<sub>2</sub> into the product. Write the product from the ion charges, Ca<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup>.
The formula is right, but N does not balance: 4 on the left, 2 on the right.
Balanced, but every coefficient shares a factor of 2.

q: Strontium carbonate is heated strongly, the way limestone is heated to make lime. Which equation shows the decomposition?
h: Metal carbonate + heat → metal oxide + ?
w: SrCO3(s) → SrO(s) + CO2(g). Sr 1 = 1; C 1 = 1; O 3 = 1 + 2.
x: CO<sub>3</sub> is the carbonate ion, not a gas molecule; it cannot leave on its own.
Balanced, but metal carbonates do not decompose to the free metal and O<sub>2</sub>. They give the oxide and CO<sub>2</sub>.
This splits the formula into made-up pieces. The products are the oxide and CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: Aluminum sulfate solution (used to clarify drinking water) is mixed with barium nitrate solution. Which gives the correct formulas of the two products?
h: Keep each cation, give it the other anion, and make the charges sum to zero.
w: Al(NO3)3 and BaSO4: Al2(SO4)3(aq) + 3 Ba(NO3)2(aq) → 2 Al(NO3)3(aq) + 3 BaSO4(s).
x: These subscripts were copied from the reactants. Rebuild each formula from its ion charges.
Al(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> would have a 1+ charge left over: aluminum is Al<sup>3+</sup>, so it needs three nitrates.
A 1 : 1 ratio leaves Al<sup>3+</sup> with only one nitrate, a net 2+ charge.

q: A propane space heater run in a closed garage gets too little oxygen and makes carbon monoxide, a poison that binds hemoglobin. Which balanced equation shows this incomplete combustion of propane, C3H8?
h: Incomplete combustion gives CO. Balance C, then H, then O, and clear any fraction.
w: C3H8 → 3 CO + 4 H2O needs 7 O = 3.5 O2; double: 2 C3H8(g) + 7 O2(g) → 6 CO(g) + 8 H2O(g).
x: This is complete combustion (enough O<sub>2</sub>): the carbon becomes CO<sub>2</sub>, not CO.
The products are right, but O does not balance: 4 on the left, 3 + 4 = 7 on the right.
This keeps the coefficients for CO but writes CO<sub>2</sub>: O is 14 on the left and 20 on the right.

q: Which substance is a nonelectrolyte when dissolved in water?
h: Does it form ions? Sugars and alcohols dissolve as molecules.
w: Glucose, C6H12O6, dissolves without forming ions: a nonelectrolyte. It travels in blood as whole molecules.
x: KCl is a soluble ionic compound: it separates completely into K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>, a strong electrolyte.
Nitric acid is on the strong-acid list; it ionizes completely, a strong electrolyte.
Ammonia is a weak base: it forms a few ions, so it is a weak electrolyte.

q: A conductivity tester is dipped into three solutions, all at the same concentration. The table shows how brightly its bulb glows. Solution B is most likely which substance?
h: Bright = many ions (strong); dim = few ions (weak); none = no ions (nonelectrolyte).
w: Dim glow = weak electrolyte = acetic acid. A could be KCl or HCl; C could be sucrose.
x: KCl is a soluble ionic compound that separates completely; it would glow brightly, like solution A.
Sucrose forms no ions, so it would not light the bulb at all, like solution C.
HCl is a strong acid that ionizes completely; it would glow brightly.

q: Calcium nitrate is a fertilizer used on Valley crops. Which equation shows what happens when it dissolves in water?
h: Polyatomic ions stay intact; subscripts outside the parentheses give the number of ions.
w: When an ionic compound dissolves, it separates into its ions, and polyatomic ions stay whole. The subscript 2 outside the parentheses means two nitrate ions: Ca(NO3)2(s) → Ca2+(aq) + 2 NO3−(aq). The charges balance: +2 and 2(−1).
x: The subscript 2 means two NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ions. With only one, the charges do not balance.
Nitrate is a polyatomic ion; it stays together as NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> when the salt dissolves.
The subscript outside the parentheses counts separate ions; it does not join them into one 2− ion.

q: A barium contrast agent must be insoluble, so that almost no toxic Ba2+ dissolves and is absorbed. By the solubility rules, which barium compound is insoluble?
h: Check each anion's row and whether Ba<sup>2+</sup> is listed as an exception.
w: BaSO4 is insoluble (sulfate with Ba2+), which is why it is used for X-ray contrast. (Context only.)
x: Chlorides are soluble unless the cation is Ag<sup>+</sup>, Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>, or Pb<sup>2+</sup>; BaCl<sub>2</sub> dissolves (and is toxic).
Nitrates are always soluble, with no exceptions, so Ba(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> dissolves and would release toxic Ba<sup>2+</sup>.
Sulfides are insoluble except with Group 1, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Sr<sup>2+</sup>, and Ba<sup>2+</sup>; barium is one of the exceptions, so BaS dissolves.

q: Which pair contains two insoluble compounds?
h: "What's the H.A.P. with the heavy halides?" Which cations make insoluble chlorides, bromides, and iodides?
w: Pb2+ and Hg22+ are halide exceptions, so PbI2 and Hg2Cl2 are both insoluble.
x: PbI<sub>2</sub> is insoluble, but ZnCl<sub>2</sub> is soluble; Zn<sup>2+</sup> is not a chloride exception.
AgCl is insoluble, but every nitrate, including AgNO<sub>3</sub>, is soluble.
CaF<sub>2</sub> is insoluble (fluoride with Ca<sup>2+</sup>), but NaF is soluble (Group 1).

q: Hard-water scale is calcium carbonate. It forms the same way it does when calcium nitrate solution is mixed with potassium carbonate solution. What is the net ionic equation?
h: Write the complete ionic equation, cancel ions that are identical on both sides, and keep what is left.
w: Complete ionic: Ca2+ + 2 NO3− + 2 K+ + CO32− → CaCO3(s) + 2 K+ + 2 NO3−. Net: Ca2+(aq) + CO32−(aq) → CaCO3(s).
x: This is the molecular equation. The net ionic equation leaves out the spectator ions.
These are the spectators. They are the ions that do not react.
This splits the precipitate into ions. A solid stays together; it is the thing that forms.

q: Zinc chloride solution is mixed with potassium sulfide solution, forming a white precipitate. What is the complete ionic equation?
c: Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2 Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq) + 2 K<sup>+</sup>(aq) + S<sup>2−</sup>(aq) → ZnS(s) + 2 K<sup>+</sup>(aq) + 2 Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq)
Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2 Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq) + 2 K<sup>+</sup>(aq) + S<sup>2−</sup>(aq) → Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + S<sup>2−</sup>(aq) + 2 K<sup>+</sup>(aq) + 2 Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq)
Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq) + K<sup>+</sup>(aq) + S<sup>2−</sup>(aq) → ZnS(s) + K<sup>+</sup>(aq) + Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq)
Zn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>2−</sup>(aq) + K<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>(aq) + S<sup>2−</sup>(aq) → ZnS(s) + K<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>2−</sup>(aq)
h: Molecular first: ZnCl<sub>2</sub>(aq) + K<sub>2</sub>S(aq) → ZnS(s) + 2 KCl(aq). Then split only the (aq) compounds.
w: Zn2+(aq) + 2 Cl−(aq) + 2 K+(aq) + S2−(aq) → ZnS(s) + 2 K+(aq) + 2 Cl−(aq)
x: This splits the precipitate. ZnS is a solid and must stay as ZnS(s).
The counts are wrong: ZnCl<sub>2</sub> gives two Cl<sup>−</sup>, and K<sub>2</sub>S gives two K<sup>+</sup>.
Subscripts count separate ions; they do not make new ions such as Cl<sub>2</sub><sup>2−</sup>.

q: Which pair of solutions gives no reaction when mixed?
h: For each pair, swap partners and check both products.
w: 2 KNO3 + MgCl2 → 2 KCl(aq) + Mg(NO3)2(aq): all ions are spectators, so KNO3 and MgCl2 give no reaction.
x: Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> would precipitate: hydroxide with Mg<sup>2+</sup> is insoluble.
Mg<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> would precipitate: phosphates are insoluble except with Group 1 and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.
AgCl would precipitate: chloride with Ag<sup>+</sup> is an exception.

q: Struvite kidney stones contain magnesium and phosphate ions. In the lab, magnesium phosphate precipitates when magnesium chloride solution is mixed with sodium phosphate solution. What is the net ionic equation?
c: 3 Mg<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2 PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>(aq) + 6 Na<sup>+</sup>(aq) + 6 Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq) → Mg<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>(s) + 6 Na<sup>+</sup>(aq) + 6 Cl<sup>−</sup>(aq)
h: Find the precipitate's formula from charges, then keep only the ions that form it.
w: 3 MgCl2(aq) + 2 Na3PO4(aq) → Mg3(PO4)2(s) + 6 NaCl(aq); net: 3 Mg2+(aq) + 2 PO43−(aq) → Mg3(PO4)2(s).
x: MgPO<sub>4</sub> is not neutral (+2 and −3). The formula must come from the charges.
This is the complete ionic equation. The spectators Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> must be cancelled.
Magnesium phosphate is insoluble (phosphate, and Mg is not Group 1), so it is a solid, (s), not (aq).

q: Sulfuric acid is neutralized by lithium hydroxide: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq) + 2 LiOH(aq) → 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(l) + Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq). What is the net ionic equation?
h: Split the strong acid and the soluble base and salt, cancel spectators, then reduce.
w: H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l), the same for every strong acid + strong base.
x: Correct species, but the coefficients share a factor of 2. Reduce the net ionic equation.
H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is a strong acid, so in an ionic equation it is split into 2 H<sup>+</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>.
Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is soluble (Group 1), so Li<sup>+</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> are spectators.

q: Milk of magnesia is a suspension of solid magnesium hydroxide that neutralizes stomach acid (HCl). What is the net ionic equation?
h: Hydroxides are insoluble except with Group 1 and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>. Keep the solid together.
w: Complete ionic: Mg(OH)2(s) + 2 H+ + 2 Cl− → Mg2+ + 2 Cl− + 2 H2O. Net: Mg(OH)2(s) + 2 H+(aq) → Mg2+(aq) + 2 H2O(l). (Context only.)
x: This splits the solid hydroxide into ions. An insoluble base is written as its formula with (s).
This is the molecular equation; HCl and MgCl<sub>2</sub> are strong electrolytes and are split, leaving Cl<sup>−</sup> as a spectator.
Two OH<sup>−</sup> need two H<sup>+</sup>; here H, O, and charge do not balance.

q: After swapping partners for potassium carbonate + nitric acid, a student writes carbonic acid, H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>(aq), as a product. What should it be replaced with?
c: Nothing; H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>(aq) is the final product.
h: Which three "products" must always be rewritten as a gas plus water?
w: H2CO3 → CO2(g) + H2O(l): K2CO3(aq) + 2 HNO3(aq) → 2 KNO3(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g).
x: Atoms add up, but carbonic acid breaks into CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O, not carbon monoxide and peroxide.
Neutral CO<sub>3</sub> is not a real compound (carbonate is the CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> ion), and carbonic acid does not release H<sub>2</sub>.
H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is one of the three products that should never be a final answer.

q: Spreading an ammonium fertilizer together with a strong base wastes nitrogen as ammonia gas. Which equation correctly shows ammonium sulfate reacting with potassium hydroxide?
h: Swap, replace NH<sub>4</sub>OH, then balance.
w: Swap partners: K+ pairs with SO42−, and NH4+ pairs with OH−. NH4OH is unstable and is written as NH3(g) + H2O(l), which is the nitrogen lost as gas. Two NH4+ need 2 KOH, giving 2 H2O and 2 NH3; K2SO4 is soluble.
x: NH<sub>4</sub>OH is unstable and must be rewritten as NH<sub>3</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l).
The products are right, but K, N, and H do not balance: 2 K on the right needs 2 KOH.
K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is soluble (Group 1), so it stays (aq).

q: Solid iron(II) sulfide reacts with hydrochloric acid and gives off a rotten-egg smell. Which is the balanced equation?
h: Swap partners: Fe<sup>2+</sup> with Cl<sup>−</sup>, H<sup>+</sup> with S<sup>2−</sup>.
w: This is a double displacement: Fe2+ pairs with Cl− (FeCl2, soluble) and H+ pairs with S2− (H2S, the rotten-egg gas). Two Cl are needed, so use 2 HCl: FeS(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → FeCl2(aq) + H2S(g).
x: SO<sub>2</sub> comes from sulfites (SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>). There is no oxygen in FeS or HCl, so O cannot balance.
Balanced, but this is a double displacement: the partners swap and H<sub>2</sub>S forms; no element is released.
FeCl<sub>2</sub> is soluble (Fe<sup>2+</sup> is not a chloride exception), so it is (aq).

q: Which of these solutions gives no reaction when it is mixed with nitric acid, HNO3(aq)?
h: A double displacement needs a precipitate, water, or a gas.
w: KCl: HNO3(aq) + KCl(aq) would give only HCl(aq) and KNO3(aq), so all four ions are spectators and there is no reaction.
x: An acid and a base make water: a neutralization.
Acid + carbonate makes H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, which releases CO<sub>2</sub> gas.
